title: Quantifying (non-)weak compactness of operators on \(AL\)- and \(C(K)\)-spaces
author: Antonio Acuaviva and Amir Bahman Nasseri
abstract: We study the representation of non-weakly compact operators between \(AL\)-spaces. In this setting, we show that every operator admits a best approximant in the ideal of weakly compact operators. Using duality arguments, we extend this result to operators between \(C(L)\)-spaces where \(L\) is extremally disconnected. We also characterize the weak essential norm for operators between \(AL\)-spaces in terms of factorizations of the identity on \(\ell_{1}\). As a consequence, we deduce that the weak Calkin algebra \(\mathscr{B}(E)/\mathscr{W}(E)\) admits a unique algebra norm for every \(AL\)-space \(E\). By duality, similar results are obtained for \(C(K)\)-spaces. In particular, we prove that for operators \(T:L_{\infty}[0,1]\to L_{\infty}[0,1]\) the weak essential norm, the residuum norm, and the De Blasi measure of weak compactness coincide, answering a question of González, Saksman and Tylli.

1.

Introduction and Main Results

−

A Banach lattice \(E\) is said to be an Abstract Lebesgue space (\(AL\)-space) if it behaves like the classical \(L_{1}\)-spaces, in other words, if \(\lVert x+y\rVert=\lVert x\rVert+\lVert y\rVert\) for every \(x,y\in E^{+}\), the positive cone of \(E\). Important examples of \(AL\)-spaces naturally include \(L_{1}\)-spaces and the spaces \(\mathcal{M}(K)\) of Borel regular measures on compact Hausdorff spaces \(K\). In fact, from the remarkable representation theorems of Kakutani (see, for example ), every \(AL\)-space can be represented (up to a lattice isometry) by an \(L_{1}\)-space, where the underlying measure space is strictly localizable (see Definition 3.3). Thus, the study of \(AL\)-spaces reduces to the study of \(L_{1}\)-spaces with an underlying strictly localizable measure space. The same holds in the complex setting: using complex Banach lattices, every complex \(AL\)-space admits a representation as an \(L_{1}\)-space (see ) with underlying strictly localizable measure space. In particular, for any measure space \((X,\Sigma,\mu)\), since \(L_{1}(X,\Sigma,\mu)\) is an \(AL\)-space, there exists a strictly localizable measure space \((X^{\prime},\Sigma^{\prime},\mu^{\prime})\) such that \(L_{1}(X,\Sigma,\mu)\) and \(L_{1}(X^{\prime},\Sigma^{\prime},\mu^{\prime})\) are lattice isometrically isomorphic; for this special case, the construction of this lattice isometry can be explicitly found, for example, in the proof of . Consequently, requiring the measure space to be strictly localizable entails no loss of generality, and our results therefore remain valid for any measure space \((X,\Sigma,\mu)\).

The study of weak compactness in \(AL\)-spaces is classical in Banach space theory. Early works include those of Dunford and Pettis and Grothendieck’s characterization of weak compactness in \(\mathcal{M}(K)\) spaces . In recent years, there has been growing interest in the quantitative study of weak compactness (see, for example, ), leading to quantitative versions of classical results with consequences that cannot be directly deduced from the original statements. It is within this context that we situate our work.

Let us recall that an operator \(T:E\to F\) is weakly compact if \(T[B_{E}]\), the image of the unit ball of \(E\), is a relatively weakly compact set in \(F\). We define the weak essential norm of an operator \(T:E\to F\) as the distance of the operator to the ideal \(\mathscr{W}(E,F)\) of weakly compact operators, that is

\(\lVert T\rVert_{w}=\inf\{\lVert T-W\rVert:W\in\mathscr{W}(E,F)\}.\)

We study the representation of weakly compact operators between \(AL\)-spaces and use this to give quantitative estimates of the weak essential norm. Our main results in this regard can be summarized in the following theorem.

Let \((X,\Sigma,\mu)\) and \((Y,\Gamma,\nu)\) be strictly localizable measure spaces, and \(T:L_{1}(X,\Sigma,\mu)\to L_{1}(Y,\Gamma,\nu)\) be an operator. Then there exists a weakly compact operator \(W:L_{1}(X,\Sigma,\mu)\to L_{1}(Y,\Gamma,\nu)\) such that

\(\lVert T\rVert_{w}=\lVert T-W\rVert=\inf_{\Theta\subseteq Y,\nu(\Theta)<\infty}\alpha_{\Theta}(T),\)

where \(\alpha_{\Theta}(T)=\limsup_{\nu(B)\to 0,B\subseteq\Theta}\lVert\chi_{Y\backslash\Theta}T+\chi_{B}T\rVert\).

Recall that if \(K\) is a compact Hausdorff space, then the Riesz representation theorem gives \(C(K)^{*}=\mathcal{M}(K)\). A simple duality argument now allows us to obtain the following.

Let \(T:C(K)\to C(L)\) be an operator, where \(K,L\) are compact Hausdorff spaces and \(L\) is extremally disconnected. Then there exists a weakly compact operator \(W:C(K)\to C(L)\) such that

\(\lVert T^{*}\rVert_{w}=\lVert T\rVert_{w}=\lVert T-W\rVert.\)

Observe that the previous corollary applies, in particular, to \(L_{\infty}[0,1]\).

The results above fail if one considers the ideal of compact operators instead of the weakly compact operators. In this case, Feder has shown that, in general, no best approximant exists.

The previous theorem extends the main result of , which was originally proved under the assumption that \(X\) and \(Y\) are compact metric spaces, the \(\sigma\)-algebras are the Borel \(\sigma\)-algebras, and the measures are finite. We first generalize this result to arbitrary finite measure spaces, which in turn allows us to extend it further to all strictly localizable measure spaces. This broader extension has many interesting consequences for the study of non-weakly compact operators on \(AL\)- and \(C(K)\)-spaces, as we shall now discuss.

We start by giving a characterisation of the weak essential norm of operators between \(AL\)-spaces, in terms of factorizations of the identity operator on \(\ell_{1}\). We will always use the convention that the supremum of positive quantities over the empty set is zero.

Let \(E,F\) be \(AL\)-spaces and \(T:E\to F\) be an operator. Then

\(\lVert T\rVert_{w}=\sup\{\lVert U\rVert^{-1}\lVert V\rVert^{-1}:UTV=I_{\ell_{1}}\}.\)

The previous theorem may be viewed as a quantitative version of Pełczyński’s theorem on non-weakly compact operators with range in an \(AL\)-space in the special case where the domain is also an \(AL\)-space. This restriction is necessary, as no such quantitative statement involving the weak essential norm holds in general; see Example 5.6.

By duality, a similar result can be obtained for \(C(K)\)-spaces, which again provides a quantitative version of Pełczyński’s classical theorem on weakly compact operators from \(C(K)\)-spaces . Recall that the minimum modulus (also called injectivity modulus) of an operator \(T:E\to F\) is defined by

\(m(T)=\inf\{\lVert Tx\rVert:x\in E,\hskip 5.0pt\lVert x\rVert=1\}.\)

Let \(T:C(L)\to C(K)\) be an operator, where \(K,L\) are compact Hausdorff spaces. Then

\(\lVert T^{*}\rVert_{w}=\sup\{m(TV)|\hskip 5.0ptV:c_{0}\to C(L),\hskip 5.0pt\lVert V\rVert\leq 1\}.\)

In particular, if \(K\) is sequentially compact, we have

\(\lVert T^{*}\rVert_{w}=\sup\{\lVert U\rVert^{-1}\lVert V\rVert^{-1}:UTV=I_{c_{0}}\},\)

while if \(L\) is extremally disconnected

\(\lVert T^{*}\rVert_{w}=\sup\{\lVert U\rVert^{-1}\lVert V\rVert^{-1}:UTV=I_{\ell_{\infty}}\}.\)

Observe that if \(K\) is assumed to be extremally disconnected, then \(\lVert T^{*}\rVert_{w}=\lVert T\rVert_{w}\).

Factorizations of this type have appeared in the literature for a significant time (see, for instance, and the discussion following , as well as ). More recently, they have played a prominent role in the work of Johnson and Phillips ; see also the work of Arnott and Laustsen .

Once a quantitative factorization has been established, one can extract significant information about the structure of norms in the weak Calkin algebra. Recall that an algebra norm \(\lVert\cdot\rVert\) on an algebra \(\mathcal{A}\) is minimal (respectively, maximal) if for any other algebra norm \({\left|\kern-1.07639pt\left|\kern-1.07639pt\left|\cdot\right|\kern-1.07639pt\right|\kern-1.07639pt\right|}\) on \(\mathcal{A}\), there exists a constant \(c>0\) such that \(c\lVert\cdot\rVert\leq{\left|\kern-1.07639pt\left|\kern-1.07639pt\left|\cdot\right|\kern-1.07639pt\right|\kern-1.07639pt\right|}\) (respectively, there exists \(C>0\) such that \({\left|\kern-1.07639pt\left|\kern-1.07639pt\left|\cdot\right|\kern-1.07639pt\right|\kern-1.07639pt\right|}\leq C\lVert\cdot\rVert\)).

We say that an algebra \(\mathcal{A}\) admits a unique algebra norm if it possesses a norm that is both maximal and minimal. In this case, all algebra norms on \(\mathcal{A}\) induce the same topology; that is, there is a unique topology arising from algebra norms. We emphasize that completeness of the algebra norms is not assumed. Using our factorization results, we obtain the following.

Let \(E\) be an \(AL\)-space. Then the weak Calkin algebra \(\mathscr{B}(E)/\mathscr{W}(E)\) admits a unique algebra norm.

Let \(L\) be an extremally disconnected compact Hausdorff space. Then the weak essential norm, \(\lVert\cdot\rVert_{w}\), is minimal on the weak Calkin algebra \(\mathscr{B}(C(L))/\mathscr{W}(C(L))\).

Let \(K\) be a sequentially compact and compact Hausdorff space. Then the dual weak essential norm, \(T\mapsto\lVert T^{*}\rVert_{w}\), is minimal on the weak Calkin algebra \(\mathscr{B}(C(K))/\mathscr{W}(C(K))\).

We note that Corollary 1.9 gives a partial answer to a problem posed by Tylli, see , who asked whether the weak essential norm is minimal on the weak Calkin algebra \(\mathscr{B}(C([0,1]))/\mathscr{W}(C([0,1]))\). This naturally leads to the following question.

Is the weak essential norm dual for the weak Calkin algebra \(\mathscr{B}(C[0,1])/\mathscr{W}(C[0,1])\), in other words, does there exists \(c>0\) such that \(\lVert T^{*}\rVert_{w}\geq c\lVert T\rVert_{w}\) for all \(T\in\mathscr{B}(C([0,1]))\)?

Another property of interest in the study of algebra norms, this time of an isometric nature, is Bonsall’s minimality property (see ). A norm \(\lVert\cdot\rVert\) on an algebra \(\mathcal{A}\) is said to have Bonsall’s minimality property if, for any other algebra norm \({\left|\kern-1.07639pt\left|\kern-1.07639pt\left|\cdot\right|\kern-1.07639pt\right|\kern-1.07639pt\right|}\) satisfying \({\left|\kern-1.07639pt\left|\kern-1.07639pt\left|\cdot\right|\kern-1.07639pt\right|\kern-1.07639pt\right|}\leq\lVert\cdot\rVert\), we have equality \({\left|\kern-1.07639pt\left|\kern-1.07639pt\left|\cdot\right|\kern-1.07639pt\right|\kern-1.07639pt\right|}=\lVert\cdot\rVert\). We obtain the following.

Let \(E\) be an \(AL\)-space. Then the weak essential norm has Bonsall’s minimality property on the weak Calkin algebra \(\mathscr{B}(E)/\mathscr{W}(E)\).

In passing, we note that this corollary is a consequence of a more general result about measures of weak noncompactness in \(AL\)-spaces, see Proposition 5.11 for details.

Let \(L\) be an extremally disconnected compact Hausdorff space. Then the weak essential norm has Bonsall’s minimality property on the weak Calkin algebra \(\mathscr{B}(C(L))/\mathscr{W}(C(L))\).

Let \(K\) be a sequentially compact and compact Hausdorff space. Then the dual weak essential norm, \(T\mapsto\lVert T^{*}\rVert_{w}\), has Bonsall’s minimality property on the weak Calkin algebra \(\mathscr{B}(C(K))/\mathscr{W}(C(K))\).

We observe that the same results about general measures of weak noncompactness can also be established in the case of \(C(L)\)-spaces, where \(L\) is an extremally disconnected compact Hausdorff space (and dual ones in the case when \(K\) is sequentially compact).

Of particular interest, the previous results give information about the De Blasi measure of weak noncompactness and the residuum norm. Let us recall that, for a subset \(A\) of a Banach space \(E\), we define the De Blasi measure of weak noncompactness of \(A\) by

\(\omega(A)=\inf\{\varepsilon>0:A\subseteq D+\varepsilon B_{E},D\subseteq E\text{ weakly compact}\}.\) (1)

The function \(\omega(\cdot)\) was introduced by De Blasi , who showed that \(\omega(A)=0\) if and only if \(A\) is relatively weakly compact. For an operator \(T:E\to F\), we naturally define \(\omega(T)=\omega(TB_{E})\).

For a Banach space \(E\), denote by \(E^{co}\) the quotient space \(E^{**}/E\). The residuum operator of the operator \(T:E\to F\) is the operator \(T^{co}:E^{co}\to F^{co}\) defined by

\(T^{co}(x+E):=T^{**}(x)+F,\)

where \(x\in F^{**}\). In the literature, this operator has also been denoted by \(R(T)\). It satisfies \(\lVert T^{co}\rVert\leq\lVert T\rVert\), and \(T^{co}=0\) if and only if \(T\) is weakly compact. Residuum operators have been extensively studied and play an important role in the theory of Tauberian operators; see, for instance, .

As an immediate consequence of Corollary 1.12, we obtain information about these quantities, answering questions of Tilly and González, Saksman and Tylli .

Let \(T:L_{\infty}[0,1]\to L_{\infty}[0,1]\) be an operator. Then

\(\lVert T\rVert_{w}=\lVert T^{*}\rVert_{w}=\lVert T^{co}\rVert=\omega(T).\)

Before concluding the introduction, we would like to remark that, by the aforementioned theorems of Pełczyński, the ideals of weakly compact, strictly singular, and strictly cosingular operators coincide for \(AL\)-spaces. Consequently, any of our results concerning measures of weak noncompactness can be applied to measures of strict singularity or strict cosingularity. In the case of \(C(K)\)-spaces, the ideals of weakly compact and strictly singular operators coincide, and thus the same can be said for measures of strict singularity.

2.

Organization and notation

−

We follow standard notational conventions. By an operator, we mean a bounded linear map between normed spaces. For Banach spaces \(E\) and \(F\), we denote by \(\mathscr{B}(E,F)\) the space of bounded operators from \(E\) to \(F\), and by \(\mathscr{W}(E,F)\) the ideal of weakly compact operators. When \(E=F\), we write simply \(\mathscr{B}(E)\) and \(\mathscr{W}(E)\). We write \(\lVert T\rVert_{w}\) for the weak essential norm of an operator \(T\in\mathscr{B}(E,F)\), that is

\(\lVert T\rVert_{w}=\lVert T+\mathscr{W}(E,F)\rVert=\inf\{\lVert T-W\rVert:W\in\mathscr{W}(E,F)\}.\)

We will denote by \(B_{E}\) the unit ball of the Banach space \(E\). We also denote by \(I_{E}\) the identity operator on \(E\); when the context is clear, we simply write \(I\).

We denote by \((X,\Sigma,\mu)\) a measure space, where \(X\) is a set, \(\Sigma\) is a \(\sigma\)-algebra on \(X\), and \(\mu\) is a measure defined on \(\Sigma\). As usual, \(L_{1}(X,\Sigma,\mu)\) denotes the Banach space of equivalence classes of \(\mu\)-integrable functions.

For \(A\in\Sigma\), we denote by \(\mathds{1}_{A}\) the indicator function of \(A\). We write \(\chi_{A}\) for the operator

\(\chi_{A}:L_{1}(X,\Sigma,\mu)\to L_{1}(A,\tilde{\Sigma},\mu),\hskip 10.0pt\chi_{A}(f)=\mathds{1}_{A}f,\)

where \(\tilde{\Sigma}=\{B\cap A:B\in\Sigma\}\).

Occasionally, we use \(:=\) or \(=:\) to stress that a term is being defined; for example, we write \(L_{1}(X,\Sigma,\mu)=:E\) to emphasize that \(E\) is defined by the expression on the left. More specialized notation will be introduced as and when needed.

We give an outline of the structure of this paper. In Section 3 we introduce some background material and associated terminology. Specifically, we introduce notation and known results about Riesz spaces, measure theory, integral and singular operators, and weak compactness in finite measure spaces. Section 4 is devoted to the proof of Theorem 1.1 and also contains the proof of Corollary 1.2. For notational convenience, all results in this section are stated exclusively for the real case; however, the reader may verify that they extend easily to the complex case with the natural modifications.

Section 5 discusses the consequences of Theorem 4.18 for the weak Calkin algebra of \(AL\)-spaces. This section includes the proofs of Theorem 1.4 and Corollaries 1.7 and 1.11, as well as a brief aside on a general notion of measures of weak noncompactness for operators between \(AL\)-spaces, which may be of independent interest.

Finally, Section 6 addresses the consequences of Theorem 1.1 for the weak Calkin algebra of \(C(K)\)-spaces. It contains the proofs of Theorem 1.5 and Corollaries 1.8, 1.9, 1.12, and 1.13.

Preliminaries

3.1.

Aspects about Riesz spaces.

−

We start with a very brief overview of normed Riesz spaces and Banach lattices; for a more detailed introduction, we refer the reader to , and .

An ordered vector space \(E\) is called a Riesz space if for any pair of elements \(x,y\in E\), its supremum exists. We denote by \(x\vee y:=\sup\{x,y\}\) and \(x\wedge y:=\inf\{x,y\}\). A Riesz space \(E\) is called Dedekind complete if every bounded set \(A\subseteq E\) admits a supremum.

A Riesz space is said to have the countable sup property if whenever an arbitrary subset \(A\) has a supremum, then there exists an at most countable subset \(C\subseteq A\) such that \(\sup(C)=\sup(A)\). We note that we have the following, see .

Let \((X,\Sigma,\mu)\) be a \(\sigma\)-finite measurable space. Then \(L_{1}(X,\Sigma,\mu)\) has the countable sup property.

Given an element \(x\) of a Riesz space \(E\), we denote by \(|x|:=x\vee(-x)\) the modulus of \(x\). Two elements \(x,y\in E\) are called orthogonal, and denoted \(x\perp y\), if \(|x|\wedge|y|=0\). This is equivalent to saying that \(|x-y|=|x+y|\). For \(x,y\in E\) with \(x\leq y\) then the order interval \([x,y]\) is defined as \([x,y]:=\{x\in E:x\leq z\leq y\}\). A subspace \(A\subseteq E\) is called an order ideal if for \(y\in A\) and \(|x|\leq|y|\) we have \(x\in A\), or equivalently the order interval \([0,|y|]\subseteq A\) for \(y\in A\). Let \(\{x_{\alpha}\}\) be a net in a Riesz space. A subset \(A\) of a Riesz space is said to be order closed, if for an order convergent net \(\{x_{\alpha}\}\subseteq A\) with limit \(x\) (in symbols \(x_{\alpha}\overset{o}{\rightarrow}x\) ) we have \(x\in A\). For the definition of order convergence, we refer the reader to .

An order closed ideal is called a band. The disjoint complement of a subset \(A\subseteq E\), denoted by \(A^{d}\), is defined by

\(A^{d}=\{x\in E\ :\ |x|\wedge|y|=0\text{ for each }y\in A\}.\)

A band \(A\) is called a projection band if \(A\oplus A^{d}=E\) holds. The corresponding projection to this decomposition is called band projection. In a Dedekind complete Riesz space, every band is a projection band, see .

If \(E\) is a Riesz space, then the set of all positive elements is denoted by \(E^{+}:=\{x\in E\ |\ x\geq 0\}\), and is called the positive cone. If \(T\) is a linear map between two ordered vector spaces, then \(T\) is called positive if \(T(x)\geq 0\) for all \(x\in E^{+}\). The vector space of all linear maps from \(E\) to \(F\), where \(F\) is another ordered vector space, will be denoted by \(\mathcal{L}(E,F)\), with the order \(T\geq S\) whenever \(T(x)\geq S(x)\) for all \(x\in E^{+}\).

A linear map \(T\in\mathcal{L}(E,F)\) is called regular if it can be written as the difference of two positive linear maps. If \(T\) is regular and \(F\) is Dedekind complete then the modulus of \(|T|\) exists and \(T=T^{+}-T^{-}\), where \(T^{+}\) (called the positive part) and \(T^{-}\) (called the negative part) are positive linear maps. We denote by \(\mathcal{L}_{r}(E,F)\) the set of all regular linear maps. If \(F\) is Dedekind complete then \(\mathcal{L}_{r}(E,F)\) is also Dedekind complete, see .

We say that a linear map \(\Psi:E\to F\) is a lattice homomorphism if \(\Psi x\wedge\Psi y=0\) whenever \(x\wedge y=0\). A bijective lattice homomorphism is called a lattice isomorphism. Observe that lattice isomorphisms preserve projection bands.

A linear map \(T:E\rightarrow F\) between two Riesz spaces is called order continuous if \(x_{\alpha}\overset{o}{\rightarrow}x\) implies \(Tx_{\alpha}\overset{o}{\rightarrow}x\) for any order converging net \(\{x_{\alpha}\}\). A linear map \(T:E\rightarrow F\) between two Riesz spaces is called interval preserving if \(T\) is positive and \(T([0,x])=[0,T(x)]\).

Let \(E,F\) be Riesz-spaces and \(\Psi:E\rightarrow F\) a lattice isomorphism. Then \(\Psi\) is both order continuous and interval preserving.

3.2.

Measure theoretic aspects.

−

We recall the following definition, see for example.

A measure space \((X,\Sigma,\mu)\) is called strictly localizable or decomposable if the following holds:

  1. (a)

    \(X=\bigcup_{i\in I}X_{i}\), where \(X_{i}\in\Sigma\) are mutually disjoint measurable sets such that \(\mu(X_{i})<\infty\) for every \(i\in I\).

  2. (b)

    A set \(A\subseteq X\) is measurable if and only if \(A\cap X_{i}\) is measurable for every \(i\in I\).

  3. (c)

    For every \(A\in\Sigma\) we have \(\mu(A)=\sum_{i\in I}\mu(A\cap X_{i})\).

We call the family \(((X_{i},\Sigma_{i},\mu))_{i\in I}\) a decomposition of \((X,\Sigma,\mu)\) where \(\Sigma_{i}=\{A\cap X_{i}:A\in\Sigma\}\).

Observe that every \(\sigma\)-finite measure space is strictly localizable.

If \((X,\Sigma,\mu)\) is strictly localizable, then the decomposition \(((X_{i},\Sigma_{i},\mu))_{i\in I}\) also gives a decomposition of the space \(L_{1}(X,\Sigma,\mu)\). Indeed, we have a decomposition

\(L_{1}(X,\Sigma,\mu)=\left(\bigoplus_{i\in I}L_{1}(X_{i},\Sigma_{i},\mu)\right)_{\ell_{1}},\)

so that any \(f\in L_{1}(X,\Sigma,\mu)\) can be expressed as \(f=\sum_{i\in I}P_{i}f\), where \(P_{i}\) is the canonical projection onto \(L_{1}(X_{i},\Sigma_{i},\mu)\) and the sum is absolutely convergent.

Let \((X,\Sigma,\mu)\) be a measure space. The measure algebra induced by \((X,\Sigma,\mu)\) is the algebra of sets in \(\Sigma\) modulo null sets. We denote this algebra by \(\Sigma_{\mu}\).

Throughout the text, we will write \(A\in\Sigma_{\mu}\) to refer to the equivalence class of \(A\in\Sigma\) whenever appropriate. Algebraic operations in \(\Sigma_{\mu}\) carry over naturally from \(\Sigma\), and we continue to use the same symbols for the operations in the induced measure algebra as in the original \(\sigma\)-algebra. This convention allows us to manipulate elements of the measure algebra while conveniently referring to representatives in \(\Sigma\). It is also consistent with the structure of \(L_{1}\)-spaces, since \(\mathds{1}_{A}\) denotes the indicator function of the set \(A\) up to null sets.

Let \(\Sigma_{\mu}\) and \(\tilde{\Sigma}_{\tilde{\mu}}\) be measure algebras. We say that \(\Sigma_{\mu}\) and \(\tilde{\Sigma}_{\tilde{\mu}}\) are isomorphic if there exists a bijection \(\phi:\Sigma_{\mu}\to\tilde{\Sigma}_{\tilde{\mu}}\) such that

\(\phi(A\backslash B)=\phi(A)\backslash\phi(B),\hskip 5.0pt\text{ }\hskip 5.0pt\phi\left(\bigcup_{n=1}^{\infty}A_{n}\right)=\bigcup_{n=1}^{\infty}\phi(A_{n}),\hskip 5.0pt\text{ and }\hskip 5.0pt\mu(A)=\tilde{\mu}(\phi(A))\)

for every \(A,B\in\Sigma_{\mu}\), \((A)_{n=1}^{\infty}\subseteq\Sigma_{\mu}\).

Observe that if \(\Sigma_{\mu}\) and \(\tilde{\Sigma}_{\tilde{\mu}}\) are isomorphic measure algebras induced by \((X,\Sigma,\mu)\) and \((\tilde{X},\tilde{\Sigma},\tilde{\mu})\) respectively, then the isomorphism \(\phi:\Sigma_{\mu}\to\tilde{\Sigma}_{\tilde{\mu}}\) induces an isometric lattice isomorphism \(\Phi:L_{1}(X,\Sigma,\mu)\to L_{1}(\tilde{X},\tilde{\Sigma},\tilde{\mu})\) such that \(\Phi(\mathds{1}_{A})=\mathds{1}_{\phi(A)}\) for every \(A\in\Sigma\).

Given a family of subsets \((A_{i})_{i\in I}\) with \(A_{i}\subseteq X\), we denote by \(\sigma(\{A_{i}:i\in I\})\) the \(\sigma\)-algebra generated by this family, that is, the smallest \(\sigma\)-algebra on \(X\) containing all the sets \(A_{i}\).

A \(\sigma\)-algebra \(\Sigma\) is said to be countably generated if there exists a countable generating family \(\{A_{n}:n\in\mathbb{N}\}\subseteq\Sigma\), i.e. \(\sigma(\{A_{n}:n\in\mathbb{N}\})=\Sigma\).

We will need the following characterization of measure spaces of finite measure and countably generated \(\sigma\)-algebras; see for the non-atomic case. The atomic case follows by decomposing \(\mu\) into its atomic and non-atomic parts. We recall that a measure space \((\tilde{X},\tilde{\Sigma},\tilde{\mu})\) is called standard if \(\tilde{X}\) is a compact metric space, \(\tilde{\Sigma}\) is the \(\sigma\)-algebra of Borel sets and \(\tilde{\mu}\) is a finite measure.

Let \((X,\Sigma,\mu)\) be a measure space of finite measure and \(\Sigma\) be countably generated. Then there exists a standard measure space \((\tilde{X},\tilde{\Sigma},\tilde{\mu})\) so that \(\Sigma_{\mu}\) is isomorphic to \(\tilde{\Sigma}_{\tilde{\mu}}\).

To avoid unnecessary notation, given a measure space \((X,\Sigma,\mu)\) and a \(\sigma\)-algebra \(\tilde{\Sigma}\subseteq\Sigma\) we will still denote the restricted measure \(\mu\big|_{\tilde{\Sigma}}\) by \(\mu\), where the meaning should be clear from the context.

For future reference, we will need the following observation.

Let \((X,\Sigma,\mu)\) be a measure space and \(M\subseteq L_{1}(X,\Sigma,\mu)\) be a separable subset.

  1. (a)

    If \((X,\Sigma,\mu)\) has finite measure, then there exists a countably generated \(\sigma\)-subalgebra \(\tilde{\Sigma}\subseteq\Sigma\) such that \(L_{1}(X,\tilde{\Sigma},\mu)\) is a sublattice of \(L_{1}(X,\Sigma,\mu)\) containing \(M\).

  2. (b)

Integral operators and singular operators on \(\sigma\)-finite \(L_{1}\)-spaces.

We recall how an operator \(T:L_{1}(X,\Sigma,\mu)\to L_{1}(Y,\Gamma,\nu)\), where the underlying measure spaces are \(\sigma\)-finite, can be decomposed into its integral and singular parts. We will need the following definition, see .

Let \((X,\Sigma,\mu)\) and \((Y,\Gamma,\nu)\) be \(\sigma\)-finite measure spaces. An operator \(K:L_{1}(X,\Sigma,\mu)\rightarrow L_{1}(Y,\Gamma,\nu)\) is called an integral operator if there exists a measurable function \(k:X\times Y\rightarrow\mathbb{R}\) such that \(|k(\cdot,y)f(\cdot)|\in L_{1}(X,\Sigma,\mu)\) (\(\nu\)-a.e.) for every \(f\in L_{1}(X,\Sigma,\mu)\) and

\((Kf)(y)=\int_{X}k(x,y)f(x)d\mu(x)\hskip 15.0pt(\nu\text{-a.e.}).\)

The function \(k\) is called the kernel of the integral operator \(K\).

Observe that if \(K:L_{1}(X,\Sigma,\mu)\to L_{1}(Y,\Gamma,\nu)\) is an integral operator with kernel \(k:X\times Y\to\mathbb{R}\), then its modulus \(|K|:L_{1}(X,\Sigma,\mu)\to L_{1}(Y,\Gamma,\nu)\) is also an integral operator, with kernel \(|k|\). This follows from , together with the fact that all operators between \(AL\)-spaces are regular (2).

The following definition will also be useful throughout the paper.

Let \((X,\Sigma,\mu)\) and \((Y,\Gamma,\nu)\) be \(\sigma\)-finite measure spaces and \(K:L_{1}(X,\Sigma,\mu)\rightarrow L_{1}(Y,\Gamma,\nu)\) be an integral operator with kernel \(k\). We define the truncated integral approximations \(K_{s}\), where \(s\in\mathbb{R^{+}}\), to be the integral operators with kernel given by

\(k_{s}(x,y)=\begin{cases}\displaystyle k(x,y)&\text{if }|k(x,y)|\geq s,\\ 0&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}\)

We also refer to the kernels \(k_{s}\) as truncated kernels.

We will need the following result concerning integral operators between finite \(L_{1}\)-spaces.

Let \((X,\Sigma,\mu)\) and \((Y,\Gamma,\nu)\) be measure spaces of finite measure and \(K:L_{1}(X,\Sigma,\mu)\to L_{1}(Y,\Gamma,\nu)\) be an integral operator with kernel \(k:X\times Y\to\mathbb{R}\). Then \(k\in L_{1}(X\times Y,\Sigma\otimes\Gamma,\mu\otimes\nu)\).

Proof.Fold proof

Since \((X,\Sigma,\mu)\) is finite, we have that \(\mathds{1}_{X}\in L_{1}(X,\Sigma,\mu)\). It follows by using Remark 3.12 and Tonelli’s Theorem that

\(\int_{X\times Y}|k(x,y)|d(\mu(x)\otimes d\nu(y))=\int_{Y}\int_{X}|k(x,y)|d\mu(x)d\nu(y)=\lVert|K|\mathds{1}_{X}\rVert<\infty,\)

that is \(k\in L_{1}(X\times Y,\Sigma\otimes\Gamma,\mu\otimes\nu)\). ∎

In the following theorem, let \(E=L_{1}(X,\Sigma,\mu)\) and \(F=L_{1}(Y,\Gamma,\nu)\), where \((X,\Sigma,\mu)\) and \((Y,\Gamma,\nu)\) are \(\sigma\)-finite measure spaces. (Bukhvalov-Luxemburg-Schep-Zaanen).

The vector space \(\mathcal{L}_{\kappa}(E,F)\) is a projection band in \(\mathcal{L}_{r}(E,F)\). In particular

\(\mathscr{B}(E,F)=\mathcal{L}_{r}(E,F)=\mathcal{L}_{\kappa}(E,F)\oplus\mathcal{L}_{\kappa}(E,F)^{d}.\)

\(|S|\wedge|K|=0\text{ for all integral operators }K,\) (6)

\(|S-K|=|S+K|\text{ for all integral operators }K.\)

3.4.

Weak compactness in \(L_{1}\)-spaces.

−

We recall the following classical measure of weak noncompactness for measure spaces of finite measure.

Let \((X,\Sigma,\mu)\) be a measure space of finite measure, and let \(A\subseteq L_{1}(X,\Sigma,\mu)\) be bounded. The modulus of equi-integrability of \(A\) is defined by

\(\Delta(A)=\limsup_{\mu(B)\to 0}\sup_{f\in A}\lVert\chi_{B}f\rVert.\)

The modulus of equi-integrability is a measure of weak noncompactness of bounded subsets of \(L_{1}(X,\Sigma,\mu)\). In particular, a bounded set \(A\subseteq L_{1}(X,\Sigma,\mu)\) is relatively weakly compact if and only if \(\Delta(A)=0\), see . If \(T:E\to L_{1}(X,\Sigma,\mu)\) is an operator, we define \(\Delta(T)=\Delta(TB_{E})\) so that \(T\) is weakly compact if and only if \(\Delta(T)=0\).

We would like to emphasize that the modulus of equi-integrability, as previously defined, only characterises weak compactness for measure spaces of finite measure. Indeed, consider for example \(X=\mathbb{R}\), \(\Sigma\) its Borel \(\sigma\)-algebra and \(\lambda\) the Lebesgue measure. Then the set \(A=\{\mathds{1}_{[n,n+1]}:n\in\mathbb{N}\}\subseteq L_{1}(\mathbb{R},\Sigma,\lambda)\) is clearly not weakly compact but \(\Delta(A)=0\). Therefore, a different quantity will be needed in the general case.

4.

The proof of Theorem 1.1

−

We begin by briefly outlining the steps in the hope that this may be helpful to the reader and provide a sense of direction. The argument proceeds in four stages, according to the structure of the underlying measure spaces: we first treat standard measure spaces, then move to measure spaces of finite measure and countably generated \(\sigma\)-algebra, then to arbitrary measure spaces of finite measure, and finally to strictly localizable measure spaces.

In Section 4.1, we treat the case of standard measure spaces. This reduces to introducing a result of Weis, Theorem 4.1, which essentially establishes Theorem 1.1 in this setting.

In Section 4.2, we address measure spaces of finite measure and countably generated \(\sigma\)-algebra. The idea is to use Theorem  3.7 to reduce to the case of standard measure spaces, allowing us to apply Weis’s theorem. To ensure that this reduction works, we must show that the isomorphism preserves singular operators and the structure of kernels of integral operators. This is shown in Lemma 4.3. Using this, we establish Theorem 4.4, extending Weis’s result to finite measure spaces with countably generated \(\sigma\)-algebra.

In Section 4.3, we treat arbitrary spaces of finite measure by reducing to the previous case via two technical lemmas, Lemmas 4.8 and 4.9, which rely on the notion of rich families; see Definition 4.5. To be precise, Lemma 4.8 shows that, given a separable subset \(M\subseteq L_{1}(X,\Sigma,\mu)\) and a sequence of operators \((T_{s})_{s\in\mathbb{N}}\), we can find a \(L_{1}\)-sublattice containing \(M\) and induced by a measure space with a countably generated \(\sigma\)-algebra, while preserving the moduli \(|T_{s}|\) for all \(s\in\mathbb{N}\). Building on this, Lemma 4.9 ensures that for a singular operator \(S\) and a separable set \(M\), there exists an \(L_{1}\)-sublattice, induced by a measure space with a countably generated \(\sigma\)-algebra, which contains \(M\) and in which the restriction of \(S\) remains singular. This allows us to handle the singular part of the operator in Proposition 4.10, while Lemma 4.11 addresses the integral part. Since these are the essential ingredients we will need from the finite measure setting, we postpone the proof of the main theorem for finite measures to the next section, where it will follow as a corollary of the localized version; see Corollary 4.20.

Finally, in Section 4.4, we address the strictly localizable case. The idea is to localize the behaviour of \(T\) to an arbitrary measurable set \(\Theta\subseteq Y\) of finite measure, reduce to the finite measure case, and then show that this localized version suffices. To this end, we introduce a localized version of \(\Delta(T)\), given by \(\inf_{\Theta\subseteq Y,\nu(\Theta)<\infty}\alpha_{\Theta}(T)\), and focus on the study of \(\alpha_{\Theta}(T)\). We prove Proposition 4.17, which provides a localized representation that serves as the counterpart of the expression for \(\Delta(T)\) in the finite measure setting. Using this, we establish a localized form of the main theorem, Theorem 4.18. The rest of the section is now devoted to using this localized version to get the general one. For technical reasons, we need to explore the behaviour in \(\sigma\)-finite localized versions (instead of finite ones); note, however, that Proposition 3.10 allows us to go back to finite localizations, at least in terms of operators. In particular, we prove Proposition 4.23 which shows the existence of a best approximant, and Proposition 4.26 which establishes that

\(\lVert T\rVert_{w}=\inf_{\begin{subarray}{c}\Theta\subseteq Y,\nu(\Theta)<\infty\end{subarray}}\alpha_{\Theta}(T).\)

These two propositions yield Theorem 1.1.

4.1.

Standard measure spaces.

−

Let us focus on the particular case in which the underlying spaces \((X,\Sigma,\mu)\) and \((Y,\Gamma,\nu)\) are standard measure spaces. In this setting, for an operator \(T:L_{1}(X,\Sigma,\mu)\rightarrow L_{1}(Y,\Gamma,\nu)\), by , there exist measures \((\mu_{y})_{y\in Y}\) on \((X,\Sigma)\) such that

\((Tf)(y)=\int_{X}f(x)d\mu_{y}(x).\)

We can use Lebesgue decomposition to obtain \(\mu_{y}=\mu_{y}^{i}+\mu_{y}^{s}\) where \(\mu_{y}^{i}\) is \(\mu\)-absolutely continuous and \(\mu_{y}^{s}\) is \(\mu\)-singular. By , this gives a decomposition \(T=S+K\) defined by

\((Sf)(y)=\int_{X}f(x)d\mu^{s}_{y}(x)\hskip 5.0pt\text{ and }\hskip 5.0pt(Kf)(y)=\int_{X}f(x)d\mu^{i}_{y}(x)=\int_{X}f(x)k(x,y)d\mu(x),\)

where \(k(\cdot,y)=\frac{d\mu_{y}^{i}}{d\mu_{y}}\) is the Radon-Nikodym derivative.

There is a similar representation for \(T^{*}:L_{\infty}(Y,\Gamma,\nu)\to L_{\infty}(X,\Sigma,\mu)\) by measures \((\nu_{y})_{y\in Y}\) on \((Y,\Gamma)\) so that

\((T^{*}g)(y)=\int_{X}g(x)d\nu_{y}(x).\)

Again, we can decompose \(\nu_{y}=\nu_{y}^{i}+\nu_{y}^{s}\) where \(\nu_{y}^{i}\) is \(\nu\)-absolutely continuous and \(\nu_{y}^{s}\) is \(\nu\)-singular. Using this decomposition, the adjoint of \(S\) and \(K\) are given by

\(\displaystyle(S^{*}g)(x)=\int_{Y}g(y)d\nu^{s}_{x}(y)\hskip 5.0pt\text{ and }\hskip 5.0pt(K^{*}g)(x)=\int_{Y}g(y)d\nu^{i}_{x}(y)=\int_{Y}g(y)h(x,y)d\nu(y),\)

where \(h(x,\cdot)=\frac{d\nu_{x}^{i}}{d\nu_{x}}\) is the Radon-Nikodym derivative. The previous representations are unique and satisfy \(|\mu_{y}^{s}|\wedge|\mu_{y}^{i}|=0\) \(\nu\)-a.e. and \(|\nu_{x}^{s}|\wedge|\nu_{x}^{i}|=0\) \(\mu\)-a.e., see . By Tonelli’s theorem, one easily checks that actually \(h(x,y)=k(x,y)\).

Observe that this decomposition is a particular case of the decomposition into integral and singular part, given by Theorem 3.15. In particular, in a standard measure space, an operator is singular if and only if it has a singular representation in the sense of measures discussed before.

In the setting of standard measure spaces, Weis has shown how these representations can be used to give a formula for \(\Delta(T)\).

(Weis).

Let \((X,\Sigma,\mu)\) and \((Y,\Sigma,\nu)\) be standard measure spaces, and \(T:L_{1}(X,\Sigma,\mu)\to L_{1}(Y,\Sigma,\nu)\) be an operator. Let \((\nu_{y}^{i})_{x\in X}\) and \((\nu_{y}^{s})_{x\in X}\) be the absolutely continuous and singular parts of the measure representation of \(T^{*}\). Then there exists a weakly compact operator \(H\) such that

\(\lVert T\rVert_{w}=\lVert T-H\rVert=\Delta(T)=\inf_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\operatorname*{ess\,sup}_{x\in X}\{\rVert\nu_{x}^{s}\lVert+\int_{Y}|k_{n}(x,y)|d\nu(y)\},\)

where \(k_{n}\) are the truncated kernels

\(k_{n}(x,y)=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\frac{d\nu_{x}^{i}}{d\nu}(y)&\text{if }\left|\frac{d\nu_{x}^{i}}{d\nu}(y)\right|\geq n,\\ 0&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}\)

We note that \(k(x,y)\), as previously defined, is in fact the kernel of the integral operator \(K\) from the decomposition \(T=S+K\) given by Theorem 3.15. Using this decomposition, the previous expression for \(\Delta(T)\) can also be expressed as

\(\Delta(T)=\inf_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\operatorname*{ess\,sup}_{x\in X}\{|S|^{*}\mathds{1}_{Y}(x)+\int_{Y}|k_{n}(x,y)|d\nu(y)\}.\)

Our goal is to extend the result from standard measure spaces to measure spaces of finite measure and countably generated \(\sigma\)-algebra. This will be achieved by combining Weis’s theorem with Theorem 3.7.

We now argue that singular and integral operators are preserved under lattice isomorphisms, and how the truncated approximations of integral operators transform under such isomorphisms.

Let \((X,\Sigma,\mu)\) and \((Y,\Gamma,\nu)\) be measure spaces of finite measure with \(\Sigma\) and \(\Gamma\) countably generated. Let \(S:L_{1}(X,\Sigma,\mu)\to L_{1}(Y,\Gamma,\nu)\) be a singular operator, and \(K:L_{1}(X,\Sigma,\mu)\to L_{1}(Y,\Gamma,\nu)\) be an integral operator.

Then the operator \(\tilde{S}=S\Phi\) is a singular operator and \(\tilde{K}=K\Phi\) is an integral operator with \(\tilde{K}_{n}=K_{n}\Phi\) as its truncated integral approximations.

We now move to the setting of arbitrary finite measure spaces. We start by recalling the notion of rich families, introduced by Borwein and Moors , which will allow us to formulate the forthcoming lemmas in a unified way.

Let \(X\) be a Banach space. We say that a family \(\mathcal{R}\) of closed separable subspaces of \(X\) is rich if it satisfies the following conditions:

  1. (a)

    For every separable subset \(M\subseteq X\) there is an \(E\in\mathcal{R}\), such that \(M\subseteq E\).

  2. (b)

    For every increasing sequence \((E_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\subseteq\mathcal{R}\), the subspace \(E:=\overline{\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb{N}}E_{n}}\in\mathcal{R}\).

Recall that, as mentioned in Remark 3.8, given a measure space \((X,\Sigma,\mu)\) and \(\sigma\)-algebra \(\tilde{\Sigma}\subseteq\Sigma\), we always denote the restricted measure \(\mu|_{\tilde{\Sigma}}\) simply by \(\mu\).

Let \((X,\Sigma,\mu)\) be a finite measure space. Then Proposition 3.9 shows that

\(\displaystyle\{L_{1}(X,\tilde{\Sigma},\mu):\tilde{\Sigma}\subseteq\Sigma\text{ countably generated }\sigma\text{-algebra}\}\)

is a rich family of closed separable subspaces of \(L_{1}(X,\Sigma,\mu)\).

One advantage of rich families is that the countable intersection of rich families is again a rich family, see .

Let \(X\) be a Banach space and let \(\mathcal{R}_{n}\) be a rich family of closed separable subspaces of \(X\) for each \(n\in\mathbb{N}\). Then

\(\mathcal{R}:=\bigcap_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\mathcal{R}_{n}\)

is a rich family of closed separable subspaces of \(X\).

We focus on the singular part of the operator. Before doing so, however, we require the following technical result. From now on, if \(E\) is a closed subspace of \(L_{1}(X,\Sigma,\mu)\), we will denote by \(J_{E}:E\to L_{1}(X,\Sigma,\mu)\) the inclusion operator.

Let \((X,\Sigma,\mu)\) and \((Y,\Gamma,\nu)\) be measure spaces of finite measure. Then the following assertions hold:

  1. (i)

    For any operator \(T:L_{1}(X,\Sigma,\mu)\to L_{1}(Y,\Gamma,\nu)\) the family

    \(\displaystyle\mathcal{R}_{T}:=\{E:\hskip 3.0pt\) \(\displaystyle E=L_{1}(X,\tilde{\Sigma},\mu)\text{ for }\tilde{\Sigma}\subseteq\Sigma\text{ countably generated }\sigma\text{-algebra},\)
    \(\displaystyle\text{and }|TJ_{E}|=|T|J_{E}\}\)

    is a rich family of closed separable subspaces of \(L_{1}(X,\Sigma,\mu)\).

  2. (ii)

    For a sequence of operators \((T_{s})_{s\in\mathbb{N}}\)

    \(\mathcal{R}:=\bigcap_{s\in\mathbb{N}}\mathcal{R}_{T_{s}}\)

    is a rich family of closed separable subspaces of \(L_{1}(X,\Sigma,\mu)\), where \(\mathcal{R}_{T_{s}}\) is defined as in (i).

\((Hf)(y)=\int_{X}h(x,y)f(x)d\mu(x).\)

\(\omega(TS)=\omega(TSB_{E})\leq\|T\|\,\omega(SB_{E})=\|T\|\,\omega(S),\)

which verifies property (b) for the De Blasi measure of weak noncompactness.

For a subset \(A\subseteq E\) define

\(\operatorname{wk}_{E}(A):=\hat{\operatorname{d}}(\overline{A}^{w^{*}},E),\)

and

\(\operatorname{wck}_{E}(A):=\sup\{\operatorname{d}(\operatorname{clust}_{E^{**}}(x_{k}),E):(x_{k})\text{ is sequence in }A\},\)

where

\(\operatorname{d}(A,B)=\inf\{\lVert a-b\rVert:a\in A,b\in B\}\hskip 5.0pt\text{ and }\hskip 5.0pt\hat{\operatorname{d}}(A,B)=\sup\{d(a,B):a\in A\},\)

so that \(\operatorname{wk}_{E}(\cdot)\) and \(\operatorname{wck}_{E}(\cdot)\) are measures of weak noncompactness for sets. Proposition 5.11 and Example 5.13, together with , yield the following.

Let \(E=L_{1}(X,\Sigma,\mu)\) for a strictly localizable measure space and \(T\in\mathscr{B}(E)\). Then we have

\(\displaystyle\lVert T\rVert_{w}\) \(\displaystyle=\inf_{\Theta\subseteq Y,\nu(\Theta)<\infty}\alpha_{\Theta}(T)=\omega(TB_{E})=\operatorname{wk}_{E}(TB_{E})=\operatorname{wck}_{E}(TB_{E})\)
\(\displaystyle=\inf_{c>0,\mu(E)<\infty}\sup\{\int_{X}(|Tf|-c\mathds{1}_{E})^{+}d\mu(x):f\in B_{E}\}.\)

In the case that \(\mu\) is finite, this simplifies to

\(\displaystyle\lVert T\rVert_{w}\) \(\displaystyle=\Delta(T)=\omega(TB_{E})=\operatorname{wk}_{E}(TB_{E})=\operatorname{wck}_{E}(TB_{E})\)
\(\displaystyle=\inf_{c>0}\sup\{\int_{X}(|Tf|-c)^{+}d\mu(x):f\in B_{E})\}.\)
6.

The Weak Calkin Algebra in \(C(K)\)-spaces

−

In this section, we will show how the results of the previous section allow us to provide a proof of Theorem 1.5. Recall that for a compact Hausdorff space \(K\), we have \(C(K)^{*}=\mathcal{M}(K)\), the space of all Borel regular measures on \(K\), which is an \(AL\)-space.

We introduce the following measure of weak noncompactness in measure spaces, which originates from the seminal work of Grothendieck .

Let \(K\) be a compact Hausdorff space, and let \(A\subseteq\mathcal{M}(K)\) be a bounded subset. The modulus of uniform regularity of \(A\) is defined by

\(\varepsilon(A)=\sup\left\{\inf_{n\in\mathbb{N}}|\mu_{n}|(U_{n}):(U_{n})_{n=1}^{\infty}\text{ disjoint open subsets of }K,\ (\mu_{n})_{n=1}^{\infty}\subseteq A\right\}.\)

In particular, the classical characterisation of weak compactness of Grothendieck states that \(A\) is relatively weakly compact if and only if \(\varepsilon(A)=0\). We have the following result.

Let \(K\) be a compact Hausdorff space. Then for any operator \(T:\mathcal{M}(K)\to\mathcal{M}(K)\) we have

\(\varepsilon(TB_{\mathcal{M}(K)})=\omega(TB_{\mathcal{M}(K)})=\lVert T\rVert_{w}.\)
Proof.Fold proof

The first equality is proved in the same way as the inequalities in . Observe that the factor \(1/\pi\) appearing in their result arises from taking the supremum over \(|\mu_{n}(U_{n})|\) instead of over \(|\mu_{n}|(U_{n})\). The second equality follows directly from Proposition 5.11 and Example 5.13. ∎

We now establish the first part of Theorem 1.5, which, using the previous lemma, essentially amounts to a careful examination of the proof of Pełczyński’s theorem.

Let \(T:C(K)\to C(L)\) be an operator, where \(K,L\) are compact Hausdorff spaces. Then

\(\lVert T^{*}\rVert_{w}=\sup\{m(TV)|\hskip 5.0ptV:c_{0}\to C(L),\hskip 5.0pt\lVert V\rVert\leq 1\}.\)
Proof.Fold proof

Assume first that \(K=L\). For convenience, let

\(\eta:=\sup\{m(TV)|\hskip 5.0ptV:c_{0}\to C(L),\hskip 5.0pt\lVert V\rVert\leq 1\}.\)

We start by showing that \(\eta\leq\lVert T^{*}\rVert_{w}\). Fix \(\varepsilon>0\), by definition we can find \(V:c_{0}\to C(K)\) such that \(TV:c_{0}\to C(K)\) is an isomorphism with \(m(TV)\geq\eta-\varepsilon\). It follows that \(V^{*}T^{*}:C(L)^{*}\to\ell_{1}\) is a quotient map such that \((\eta-\varepsilon)B_{\ell_{1}}\subseteq V^{*}T^{*}[B_{\mathcal{M}(K)}]\). Consequently, for any weakly compact operator \(W\), we have

\(\displaystyle\lVert T^{*}-W\rVert\) \(\displaystyle\geq\lVert V^{*}\rVert\lVert T^{*}-W\rVert\geq\lVert V^{*}T^{*}-V^{*}W\rVert\geq\omega(V^{*}T^{*}-V^{*}W)\)
\(\displaystyle=\omega(V^{*}T^{*})\geq\eta-\varepsilon,\)

where we recall that \(\omega(\cdot)\) is the De Blasi measure of weak noncompactness (1). Taking the infimum over all weakly compact operators gives \(\lVert T^{*}\rVert_{w}\geq\eta-\varepsilon\), since \(\varepsilon\) was arbitrary, we obtain \(\lVert T^{*}\rVert_{w}\geq\eta\).

We focus now on the reverse implication. By Lemma 6.2 we have \(\varepsilon(T^{*}):=\varepsilon(T^{*}B_{\mathcal{M}(K)})=\lVert T^{*}\rVert_{w}\) for all \(T\in\mathscr{B}(C(K))\), and thus it is enough to show that \(\eta\geq\varepsilon(T^{*})\). Fix \(\varepsilon>0\). By definition of \(\varepsilon(T^{*})\) we can find a sequence of disjoint open sets \((U_{n})_{n=1}^{\infty}\) and measures \((\nu_{n})_{n=1}^{\infty}\subseteq B_{\mathcal{M}(K)}\) such that \(|T^{*}\nu_{n}|(U_{n})>\varepsilon(T^{*})-\varepsilon\) for all \(n\in\mathbb{N}\). To simplify the notation, we set \(\mu_{n}:=T^{*}\nu_{n}\).

By internal regularity, for each \(n\in\mathbb{N}\), we can find a compact subset \(F_{n}\subseteq U_{n}\) such that \(|\mu_{n}|(U_{n}\backslash F_{n})<\varepsilon\), which implies \(|\mu_{n}|(F_{n})>\varepsilon(T^{*})-2\varepsilon\).

Observe that

\(|\mu_{n}|(F_{n})=\sup\{|\int_{F_{n}}gd\mu_{n}|:g\in B_{C(K)}\},\)

so that, for each \(n\in\mathbb{N}\), we can find \(g_{n}\in B_{C(K)}\) such that \(\int_{F_{n}}g_{n}d\mu_{n}>\varepsilon(T^{*})-2\varepsilon\). By Urysohn’s lemma, there exists \(h_{n}\in C(K)\), \(0\leq h_{n}\leq 1\) such that \(h_{n}=1\) in \(F_{n}\) and \(h_{n}=0\) in \(K\backslash U_{n}\). Let \(f_{n}:=h_{n}g_{n}\) and note that

\(|\mu_{n}(f_{n})|=|\int_{K}f_{n}d\mu_{n}|=|\int_{U_{n}}h_{n}g_{n}d\mu_{n}|\geq\int_{F_{n}}g_{n}d\mu_{n}-\int_{U_{n}\backslash F_{n}}|h_{n}g_{n}|d\mu_{n}>\varepsilon(T^{*})-3\varepsilon.\)

Define the map \(V:c_{0}\to C(K)\) by \(Ve_{n}=f_{n}\), where \((e_{n})_{n=1}^{\infty}\) is the canonical basis of \(c_{0}\). Observe that, by construction, \(\lVert V\rVert\leq 1\). We have that \(TV:c_{0}\to C(K)\) satisfies

\(\displaystyle\inf_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\lVert TVe_{n}\rVert\) \(\displaystyle\geq\inf_{n\in\mathbb{N}}|\nu_{n}(TVe_{n})|=\inf_{n\in\mathbb{N}}|(T^{*}\nu_{n})(f_{n})|=\inf_{n\in\mathbb{N}}|\mu_{n}(f_{n})|>\varepsilon(T^{*})-3\varepsilon.\)

It follows from a result of Rosenthal (see , Remark 1 after Theorem 3.4) that \(TV\) is an isomorphism on a copy of \(c_{0}\). Moreover, as noted in , we can ensure that, on this copy, \(TV\) is bounded below by \(\varepsilon(T^{*})-3\varepsilon\). In other words, by restricting the domain of \(V\) to this copy, we obtain \(m(TV)>\varepsilon(T^{*})-3\varepsilon\). Since \(\varepsilon>0\) was arbitrary, we conclude that \(\eta\geq\varepsilon(T^{*})=\lVert T^{*}\rVert_{w}\), which completes the proof in the case \(K=L\).

For arbitrary compact spaces \(K\not=L\), note that \(C(K)\oplus C(L)=C(K\sqcup L)\), where the sum is taken with the \(\ell_{\infty}\)-norm and \(K\sqcup L\) denotes the topological disjoint union of \(K\) and \(L\). Naturally, we may view \(T:C(K)\to C(L)\) as an operator \(T:C(K\sqcup L)\to C(K\sqcup L)\), so the previous case and straightforward manipulations yield the result. ∎

The quantity

\(\sup\{m(TV)\;|\;V:c_{0}\to C(L),\;\|V\|\leq 1\},\)

which measures how well an operator \(T\) fixes a copy of \(c_{0}\), has also been studied for operators between arbitrary Banach spaces \(T:X\to Y\). For example, in this quantity appears under the name \(\operatorname{fix}_{c_{0}}(T)\), and it is shown that

\(\operatorname{fix}_{c_{0}}(T)=\operatorname{uc}(T)\)

, where \(\operatorname{uc}(T)\) quantifies how far \(T\) is from being unconditionally converging. Moreover, it is shown that for operators \(T:C(K)\to Y\), this quantity coincides with several other measures of weak noncompactness, see . In particular, Proposition 6.3 may be viewed as an extension of the aforementioned corollary in the case where the codomain is also a \(C(K)\)-space.

In the previous proposition, we showed that the weak essential norm of the dual operator \(T^{*}\) provides a measure of how well an operator \(T\) fixes a copy of \(c_{0}\). To obtain a factorization, we need to show that this copy is complemented with good constants (possibly after passing to a subcopy of \(c_{0}\) inside of it).

We will establish this in two general settings. First, when \(K\) is sequentially compact (for instance, if \(K\) is first countable), we will argue that every copy of \(c_{0}\) admits a further subcopy that is complemented with good constants. Second, when \(L\) is extremally disconnected, fixing a copy of \(c_{0}\) implies fixing a copy of \(\ell_{\infty}\) with the same constants.

We note that some structural assumptions on \(K\) and \(L\) are necessary. It is possible for an operator \(T:C(K)\to C(L)\) to fix a copy of \(c_{0}\) but not fix a complemented copy of \(c_{0}\) nor a copy of \(\ell_{\infty}\). For instance, by a remarkable construction of Haydon , there exists a compact Hausdorff space \(K\) such that \(C(K)\) is a Grothendieck space (hence it contains no complemented copy of \(c_{0}\), see ) not containing a copy of \(\ell_{\infty}\). In this case, no factorization of the identity of \(c_{0}\) or \(\ell_{\infty}\) is possible through the identity operator \(I_{C(K)}:C(K)\to C(K)\), while \(I_{C(K)}\) trivially fixes a copy of \(c_{0}\).

We begin with the case \(K\) sequentially compact. For this, we require a mild variation of that is better suited to our context. If \(E\) is a Banach space, a subset \(M\subseteq B_{E^{*}}\) is said to be \(1\)-norming if

\(\lVert x\rVert=\sup_{x^{*}\in M}|x^{*}(x)|.\)
(Dowling, Randrianantoanina and Turett).

Let \(E\) be a Banach space. Suppose there exists \(M\subseteq B_{E^{*}}\) \(1\)-norming and weak∗ sequentially compact. Then for any \(Y\subseteq E\), \(Y\sim c_{0}\) and any \(\varepsilon>0\), there exist \(Z\subseteq Y\) and a projection \(P:E\to Z\) such that \(Z\) is \((1+\varepsilon)\)-isometric to \(c_{0}\) and \(\lVert P\rVert\leq 1+\varepsilon\).

Proof.Fold proof

The proof is essentially that of , with natural modifications to accommodate the \(1\)-norming set \(M\). We include an outline for the reader’s convenience. Let \(\delta>0\) be chosen sufficiently small, depending on the desired \(\varepsilon\). By James’s distortion theorem (see, for example, ), there exists a sequence \((u_{n})_{n=1}^{\infty}\subseteq B_{Y}\) such that

\((1-\delta)\sup_{n\in\mathbb{N}}|a_{n}|\leq\lVert\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}a_{n}u_{n}\rVert\leq\sup_{n\in\mathbb{N}}|a_{n}|,\)

for any \((a_{n})_{n=1}^{\infty}\in c_{0}\). Choose \((u^{*}_{n})_{n=1}^{\infty}\subseteq M\) such that \(|u_{n}^{*}(u_{n})|\geq 1-\delta\). Multiplying \(u_{n}\) by an unimodular scalar number, we may assume \(u_{n}^{*}(u_{n})\geq 1-\delta\). Observe that this implies

\(|u^{*}_{n}(\sum_{m\not=n}a_{m}u_{m})|\leq\delta\) (13)

for all \((a_{m})_{m\in\mathbb{N}}\in B_{c_{0}}\) and all \(n\in\mathbb{N}\). Since \(M\) is weak∗ sequentially compact, by passing to a subsequence, we may assume \((u_{n}^{*})_{n=1}^{\infty}\) converges weak∗ to some element. Define \(w^{*}_{n}=(u_{2n}-u_{2n-1})/2\) and \(w_{n}=u_{2n}-u_{2n-1}\). It is clear that \((w^{*}_{n})_{n=1}^{\infty}\) is a weak∗ null sequence, while \(w_{n}^{*}(w_{n})\geq 1-\delta\) for all \(n\in\mathbb{N}\) and (13) still holds with \(u_{n}^{*}\) and \(u_{m}\) replaced by \(w_{n}^{*}\) and \(w_{m}\) respectively.

Define the operator \(J:c_{0}\to E\), \((a_{n})_{n=1}^{\infty}\mapsto\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}a_{n}w_{n}\) and \(Q:E\to c_{0}\), \(x\mapsto(w^{*}_{n}(x))_{n=1}^{\infty}\). It is straightforward to verify that \(\lVert I_{c_{0}}-QJ\rVert\leq 2\delta\), and thus we can find an operator \(R:c_{0}\to c_{0}\) with \(\lVert R\rVert\leq(1-2\delta)^{-1}\) such that \(RQJ=I_{c_{0}}\). It is easy to verify that \(Z=\overline{\operatorname{span}\{w_{n}:n\in\mathbb{N}\}}\subseteq Y\) is the desired copy of \(c_{0}\) and \(P=J(QR)\) the desired projection. ∎

The previous reformulation is stronger than the original version by Dowling, Randrianantoanina, and Turett, particularly in the context of \(C(K)\)-spaces. Indeed, the set \(\{\delta_{k}:k\in K\}\subseteq C(K)^{*}\) is always \(1\)-norming, so the existence of a \(1\)-norming, weak∗ sequentially compact subset of the dual unit ball is automatically satisfied whenever \(K\) is sequentially compact. In contrast, requiring the dual unit ball to be weak∗ sequentially compact can be a stronger condition. For instance, assuming the Continuum Hypothesis, Talagrand constructed a Corson compact space \(K\) that is first countable, and hence sequentially compact, but for which the unit ball of \(C(K)^{*}\) (endowed with the weak∗ topology) contains a topological copy of \(\beta\mathbb{N}\) (see ). In particular, the dual unit ball fails to be sequentially compact while \(K\) is sequentially compact. We thank Antonio Avilés for bringing this example to our attention.

The case when \(L\) is extremally disconnected will follow from a quantitative version of a result of Rosenthal, originally stated as .

(Rosenthal).

Let \(\Gamma\) be an infinite set, and let \(E\) and \(F\) be Banach spaces with \(E\) \(1\)-complemented in \(E^{**}\). Let \(T:E\to F\) and \(V:c_{0}\to E\), \(\lVert V\rVert\leq 1\), such that \(m(TV)>\delta\). Then there exists \(\tilde{V}:\ell_{\infty}\to E\) such that \(T\tilde{V}:\ell_{\infty}\to F\) satisfies \(m(T\tilde{V})>\delta\).

Proof.Fold proof

It suffices to observe that the proof of is essentially quantitative. This proposition is the key ingredient in the proof of , which now becomes quantitative upon incorporating the condition that the projection \(P:E^{**}\to E\) has norm one. ∎

As an automatic consequence, we get the stated factorization result for operators between \(C(K)\)-spaces.

Proof of Theorem 1.5.Fold proof

The first part was proven in Proposition 6.3. The second part follows automatically from the first part, which tells us that we fix a copy of \(c_{0}\) with controlled bounds, and Theorems 6.5 and 6.7.

Indeed, Theorem 6.5 guarantees that when \(K\) is sequentially compact, we can pass to a subcopy of the fixed copy of \(c_{0}\) that is complemented with good constants. On the other hand, when \(L\) is extremally disconnected, \(C(L)\) is \(1\)-complemented in its bidual; thus, by Theorem 6.7, we quantitatively fix a copy of \(\ell_{\infty}\), which is \(1\)-injective and therefore complemented with good constants.

The details are standard and hence omitted here; see, for example, the argument in . ∎

Corollaries 1.8, 1.9, 1.12, and 1.13 follow directly from Theorem 1.5. In both cases, minimality is derived from the argument in – see also –, and observe that, in contrast with the proof of Corollary 1.7, we need these arguments to bypass the need for maximality. Bonsall’s minimality property is established by the same reasoning used in the proof of . Alternatively, similar results regarding measures of weak noncompactness, akin to those in Proposition 5.11, can be obtained, which also imply Bonsall’s minimality property. Since these arguments closely follow the aforementioned ones, we omit the details. Theorem 1.14 follows immediately from these results.
