Let \((X,\Sigma,\mu)\) and \((Y,\Gamma,\nu)\) be strictly localizable measure spaces, and \(T:L_{1}(X,\Sigma,\mu)\to L_{1}(Y,\Gamma,\nu)\) be an operator. Then there exists a weakly compact operator \(W:L_{1}(X,\Sigma,\mu)\to L_{1}(Y,\Gamma,\nu)\) such that

\(\lVert T\rVert_{w}=\lVert T-W\rVert=\inf_{\Theta\subseteq Y,\nu(\Theta)<\infty}\alpha_{\Theta}(T),\)

where \(\alpha_{\Theta}(T)=\limsup_{\nu(B)\to 0,B\subseteq\Theta}\lVert\chi_{Y\backslash\Theta}T+\chi_{B}T\rVert\).

Let \(T:C(K)\to C(L)\) be an operator, where \(K,L\) are compact Hausdorff spaces and \(L\) is extremally disconnected. Then there exists a weakly compact operator \(W:C(K)\to C(L)\) such that

\(\lVert T^{*}\rVert_{w}=\lVert T\rVert_{w}=\lVert T-W\rVert.\)
The results above fail if one considers the ideal of compact operators instead of the weakly compact operators. In this case, Feder has shown that, in general, no best approximant exists.

Let \(E,F\) be \(AL\)-spaces and \(T:E\to F\) be an operator. Then

\(\lVert T\rVert_{w}=\sup\{\lVert U\rVert^{-1}\lVert V\rVert^{-1}:UTV=I_{\ell_{1}}\}.\)

Let \(T:C(L)\to C(K)\) be an operator, where \(K,L\) are compact Hausdorff spaces. Then

\(\lVert T^{*}\rVert_{w}=\sup\{m(TV)|\hskip 5.0ptV:c_{0}\to C(L),\hskip 5.0pt\lVert V\rVert\leq 1\}.\)

In particular, if \(K\) is sequentially compact, we have

\(\lVert T^{*}\rVert_{w}=\sup\{\lVert U\rVert^{-1}\lVert V\rVert^{-1}:UTV=I_{c_{0}}\},\)

while if \(L\) is extremally disconnected

\(\lVert T^{*}\rVert_{w}=\sup\{\lVert U\rVert^{-1}\lVert V\rVert^{-1}:UTV=I_{\ell_{\infty}}\}.\)
Observe that if \(K\) is assumed to be extremally disconnected, then \(\lVert T^{*}\rVert_{w}=\lVert T\rVert_{w}\).
Let \(E\) be an \(AL\)-space. Then the weak Calkin algebra \(\mathscr{B}(E)/\mathscr{W}(E)\) admits a unique algebra norm.

Let \(L\) be an extremally disconnected compact Hausdorff space. Then the weak essential norm, \(\lVert\cdot\rVert_{w}\), is minimal on the weak Calkin algebra \(\mathscr{B}(C(L))/\mathscr{W}(C(L))\).

Let \(K\) be a sequentially compact and compact Hausdorff space. Then the dual weak essential norm, \(T\mapsto\lVert T^{*}\rVert_{w}\), is minimal on the weak Calkin algebra \(\mathscr{B}(C(K))/\mathscr{W}(C(K))\).

Is the weak essential norm dual for the weak Calkin algebra \(\mathscr{B}(C[0,1])/\mathscr{W}(C[0,1])\), in other words, does there exists \(c>0\) such that \(\lVert T^{*}\rVert_{w}\geq c\lVert T\rVert_{w}\) for all \(T\in\mathscr{B}(C([0,1]))\)?
Let \(E\) be an \(AL\)-space. Then the weak essential norm has Bonsall’s minimality property on the weak Calkin algebra \(\mathscr{B}(E)/\mathscr{W}(E)\).
Let \(L\) be an extremally disconnected compact Hausdorff space. Then the weak essential norm has Bonsall’s minimality property on the weak Calkin algebra \(\mathscr{B}(C(L))/\mathscr{W}(C(L))\).

Let \(K\) be a sequentially compact and compact Hausdorff space. Then the dual weak essential norm, \(T\mapsto\lVert T^{*}\rVert_{w}\), has Bonsall’s minimality property on the weak Calkin algebra \(\mathscr{B}(C(K))/\mathscr{W}(C(K))\).

Let \(T:L_{\infty}[0,1]\to L_{\infty}[0,1]\) be an operator. Then

\(\lVert T\rVert_{w}=\lVert T^{*}\rVert_{w}=\lVert T^{co}\rVert=\omega(T).\)
Let \((X,\Sigma,\mu)\) be a \(\sigma\)-finite measurable space. Then \(L_{1}(X,\Sigma,\mu)\) has the countable sup property.
Let \(E,F\) be Riesz-spaces and \(\Psi:E\rightarrow F\) a lattice isomorphism. Then \(\Psi\) is both order continuous and interval preserving.

A measure space \((X,\Sigma,\mu)\) is called strictly localizable or decomposable if the following holds:

  1. (a)

    \(X=\bigcup_{i\in I}X_{i}\), where \(X_{i}\in\Sigma\) are mutually disjoint measurable sets such that \(\mu(X_{i})<\infty\) for every \(i\in I\).

  2. (b)

    A set \(A\subseteq X\) is measurable if and only if \(A\cap X_{i}\) is measurable for every \(i\in I\).

  3. (c)

    For every \(A\in\Sigma\) we have \(\mu(A)=\sum_{i\in I}\mu(A\cap X_{i})\).

We call the family \(((X_{i},\Sigma_{i},\mu))_{i\in I}\) a decomposition of \((X,\Sigma,\mu)\) where \(\Sigma_{i}=\{A\cap X_{i}:A\in\Sigma\}\).
Let \((X,\Sigma,\mu)\) be a measure space. The measure algebra induced by \((X,\Sigma,\mu)\) is the algebra of sets in \(\Sigma\) modulo null sets. We denote this algebra by \(\Sigma_{\mu}\).

Let \(\Sigma_{\mu}\) and \(\tilde{\Sigma}_{\tilde{\mu}}\) be measure algebras. We say that \(\Sigma_{\mu}\) and \(\tilde{\Sigma}_{\tilde{\mu}}\) are isomorphic if there exists a bijection \(\phi:\Sigma_{\mu}\to\tilde{\Sigma}_{\tilde{\mu}}\) such that

\(\phi(A\backslash B)=\phi(A)\backslash\phi(B),\hskip 5.0pt\text{ }\hskip 5.0pt\phi\left(\bigcup_{n=1}^{\infty}A_{n}\right)=\bigcup_{n=1}^{\infty}\phi(A_{n}),\hskip 5.0pt\text{ and }\hskip 5.0pt\mu(A)=\tilde{\mu}(\phi(A))\)

for every \(A,B\in\Sigma_{\mu}\), \((A)_{n=1}^{\infty}\subseteq\Sigma_{\mu}\).

A \(\sigma\)-algebra \(\Sigma\) is said to be countably generated if there exists a countable generating family \(\{A_{n}:n\in\mathbb{N}\}\subseteq\Sigma\), i.e. \(\sigma(\{A_{n}:n\in\mathbb{N}\})=\Sigma\).

Let \((X,\Sigma,\mu)\) be a measure space of finite measure and \(\Sigma\) be countably generated. Then there exists a standard measure space \((\tilde{X},\tilde{\Sigma},\tilde{\mu})\) so that \(\Sigma_{\mu}\) is isomorphic to \(\tilde{\Sigma}_{\tilde{\mu}}\).

To avoid unnecessary notation, given a measure space \((X,\Sigma,\mu)\) and a \(\sigma\)-algebra \(\tilde{\Sigma}\subseteq\Sigma\) we will still denote the restricted measure \(\mu\big|_{\tilde{\Sigma}}\) by \(\mu\), where the meaning should be clear from the context.

Let \((X,\Sigma,\mu)\) be a measure space and \(M\subseteq L_{1}(X,\Sigma,\mu)\) be a separable subset.

  1. (a)

    If \((X,\Sigma,\mu)\) has finite measure, then there exists a countably generated \(\sigma\)-subalgebra \(\tilde{\Sigma}\subseteq\Sigma\) such that \(L_{1}(X,\tilde{\Sigma},\mu)\) is a sublattice of \(L_{1}(X,\Sigma,\mu)\) containing \(M\).

  2. (b)

    If \((X,\Sigma,\mu)\) is strictly localizable, then there exist a \(\sigma\)-finite measurable set \(\Omega\subseteq X\) and a countably generated \(\sigma\)-algebra \(\hat{\Sigma}\) on \(\Omega\) such that \(L_{1}(\Omega,\hat{\Sigma},\mu)\) is a sublattice of \(L_{1}(X,\Sigma,\mu)\) containing \(M\).

Observe that, in both cases, these sublattices are \(1\)-complemented in \(L_{1}(X,\Sigma,\mu)\).

Let \((Y,\Gamma, u)\) be a strictly localizable measure space, and let \(\Theta\subseteq Y\) be a \(\sigma\)-finite measurable set with \( u(\Theta) ot=0\). Then there exists a measure \( ilde{ u}\) on \(\Gamma\) such that \((Y,\Gamma, ilde{ u})\) is strictly localizable, \( ilde{ u}(\Theta)=1\), and there is an isometric lattice isomorphism \(\Psi:L_{1}(Y,\Gamma, u) o L_{1}(Y,\Gamma, ilde{ u})\).

Furthermore, \(\Psi\) commutes with multiplication operators, i.e. for any \(h\in L_{\infty}(Y,\Gamma, u)\) and any \(f\in L_{1}(Y,\Gamma, u)\), we have \(\Psi(hf)=h\Psi(f)\), where on the right hand side \(h\) is considered as an element of \(L_{\infty}(Y,\Gamma, ilde{ u})\).

Let \((X,\Sigma,\mu)\) and \((Y,\Gamma,\nu)\) be \(\sigma\)-finite measure spaces. An operator \(K:L_{1}(X,\Sigma,\mu)\rightarrow L_{1}(Y,\Gamma,\nu)\) is called an integral operator if there exists a measurable function \(k:X\times Y\rightarrow\mathbb{R}\) such that \(|k(\cdot,y)f(\cdot)|\in L_{1}(X,\Sigma,\mu)\) (\(\nu\)-a.e.) for every \(f\in L_{1}(X,\Sigma,\mu)\) and

\((Kf)(y)=\int_{X}k(x,y)f(x)d\mu(x)\hskip 15.0pt(\nu\text{-a.e.}).\)

The function \(k\) is called the kernel of the integral operator \(K\).

Observe that if \(K:L_{1}(X,\Sigma,\mu)\to L_{1}(Y,\Gamma,\nu)\) is an integral operator with kernel \(k:X\times Y\to\mathbb{R}\), then its modulus \(|K|:L_{1}(X,\Sigma,\mu)\to L_{1}(Y,\Gamma,\nu)\) is also an integral operator, with kernel \(|k|\). This follows from , together with the fact that all operators between \(AL\)-spaces are regular (2).

Let \((X,\Sigma,\mu)\) and \((Y,\Gamma,\nu)\) be \(\sigma\)-finite measure spaces and \(K:L_{1}(X,\Sigma,\mu)\rightarrow L_{1}(Y,\Gamma,\nu)\) be an integral operator with kernel \(k\). We define the truncated integral approximations \(K_{s}\), where \(s\in\mathbb{R^{+}}\), to be the integral operators with kernel given by

\(k_{s}(x,y)=\begin{cases}\displaystyle k(x,y)&\text{if }|k(x,y)|\geq s,\\ 0&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}\)

We also refer to the kernels \(k_{s}\) as truncated kernels.

Let \((X,\Sigma,\mu)\) and \((Y,\Gamma,\nu)\) be measure spaces of finite measure and \(K:L_{1}(X,\Sigma,\mu)\to L_{1}(Y,\Gamma,\nu)\) be an integral operator with kernel \(k:X\times Y\to\mathbb{R}\). Then \(k\in L_{1}(X\times Y,\Sigma\otimes\Gamma,\mu\otimes\nu)\).

results.title: (Bukhvalov-Luxemburg-Schep-Zaanen).
results.statementHtml:
The vector space \(\mathcal{L}_{\kappa}(E,F)\) is a projection band in \(\mathcal{L}_{r}(E,F)\). In particular

\(\mathscr{B}(E,F)=\mathcal{L}_{r}(E,F)=\mathcal{L}_{\kappa}(E,F)\oplus\mathcal{L}_{\kappa}(E,F)^{d}.\)

Let \((X,\Sigma,\mu)\) be a measure space of finite measure, and let \(A\subseteq L_{1}(X,\Sigma,\mu)\) be bounded. The modulus of equi-integrability of \(A\) is defined by

\(\Delta(A)=\limsup_{\mu(B)\to 0}\sup_{f\in A}\lVert\chi_{B}f\rVert.\)

We would like to emphasize that the modulus of equi-integrability, as previously defined, only characterises weak compactness for measure spaces of finite measure. Indeed, consider for example \(X=\mathbb{R}\), \(\Sigma\) its Borel \(\sigma\)-algebra and \(\lambda\) the Lebesgue measure. Then the set \(A=\{\mathds{1}_{[n,n+1]}:n\in\mathbb{N}\}\subseteq L_{1}(\mathbb{R},\Sigma,\lambda)\) is clearly not weakly compact but \(\Delta(A)=0\). Therefore, a different quantity will be needed in the general case.

results.title: (Weis).
results.statementHtml:
Let \((X,\Sigma,\mu)\) and \((Y,\Sigma,\nu)\) be standard measure spaces, and \(T:L_{1}(X,\Sigma,\mu)\to L_{1}(Y,\Sigma,\nu)\) be an operator. Let \((\nu_{y}^{i})_{x\in X}\) and \((\nu_{y}^{s})_{x\in X}\) be the absolutely continuous and singular parts of the measure representation of \(T^{*}\). Then there exists a weakly compact operator \(H\) such that

\(\lVert T\rVert_{w}=\lVert T-H\rVert=\Delta(T)=\inf_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\operatorname*{ess\,sup}_{x\in X}\{\rVert\nu_{x}^{s}\lVert+\int_{Y}|k_{n}(x,y)|d\nu(y)\},\)

where \(k_{n}\) are the truncated kernels

\(k_{n}(x,y)=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\frac{d\nu_{x}^{i}}{d\nu}(y)&\text{if }\left|\frac{d\nu_{x}^{i}}{d\nu}(y)\right|\geq n,\\ 0&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}\)

We note that \(k(x,y)\), as previously defined, is in fact the kernel of the integral operator \(K\) from the decomposition \(T=S+K\) given by Theorem 3.15. Using this decomposition, the previous expression for \(\Delta(T)\) can also be expressed as

\(\Delta(T)=\inf_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\operatorname*{ess\,sup}_{x\in X}\{|S|^{*}\mathds{1}_{Y}(x)+\int_{Y}|k_{n}(x,y)|d\nu(y)\}.\)

Let \((X,\Sigma,\mu)\) and \((Y,\Gamma,\nu)\) be measure spaces of finite measure with \(\Sigma\) and \(\Gamma\) countably generated. Let \(S:L_{1}(X,\Sigma,\mu)\to L_{1}(Y,\Gamma,\nu)\) be a singular operator, and \(K:L_{1}(X,\Sigma,\mu)\to L_{1}(Y,\Gamma,\nu)\) be an integral operator.

  1. (i)

    Suppose \((\tilde{X},\tilde{\Sigma},\tilde{\mu})\) is a measure space such that \(\phi:\tilde{\Sigma}_{\tilde{\mu}}\to\Sigma_{\mu}\) is an isomorphism and let \(\Phi:L_{1}(\tilde{X},\tilde{\Sigma},\tilde{\mu})\to L_{1}(X,\Sigma,\mu)\) be the induced lattice isomorphism. Then the operator \(\tilde{S}=S\Phi\) is a singular operator and \(\tilde{K}=K\Phi\) is an integral operator with \(\tilde{K}_{n}=K_{n}\Phi\) as its truncated integral approximations.

  2. (ii)

    Suppose that \((\tilde{Y},\tilde{\Gamma},\tilde{\nu})\) is a measure space such that \(\psi:\Gamma_{\nu}\to\tilde{\Gamma}_{\tilde{\nu}}\) is an isomorphism and let \(\Psi:L_{1}(Y,\Gamma,\nu)\to L_{1}(\tilde{Y},\tilde{\Gamma},\tilde{\nu})\) be the induced lattice isomorphism. Then the operator \(\hat{S}=\Psi S\) is a singular operator and \(\hat{K}=\Psi K\) is an integral operator with \(\hat{K}_{n}=\Psi K_{n}\) as its truncated integral approximations.

(Countably generated \(\sigma\)-algebra case) Let \((X,\Sigma,\mu)\) and \((Y,\Gamma,\nu)\) be measure spaces of finite measure with \(\Sigma\) and \(\Gamma\) countably generated. Let \(T:L_{1}(X,\Sigma,\mu)\to L_{1}(Y,\Gamma,\nu)\) be an operator and decompose \(T=S+K\), where \(S\) is a singular operator and \(K\) is an integral operator. Then

\(\Delta(T)=\inf_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\operatorname*{ess\,sup}_{x\in X}\{|S|^{*}\mathds{1}_{Y}(x)+\int_{Y}|k_{n}(x,y)|d\nu(y)\},\)

where \(k_{n}(x,y)\) is the truncated kernel of \(K\). In particular, for a singular operator \(S\), \(\Delta(S)=\lVert S^{*}\rVert=\lVert S\rVert\).

Let \(X\) be a Banach space. We say that a family \(\mathcal{R}\) of closed separable subspaces of \(X\) is rich if it satisfies the following conditions:

  1. (a)

    For every separable subset \(M\subseteq X\) there is an \(E\in\mathcal{R}\), such that \(M\subseteq E\).

  2. (b)

    For every increasing sequence \((E_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\subseteq\mathcal{R}\), the subspace \(E:=\overline{\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb{N}}E_{n}}\in\mathcal{R}\).

Let \((X,\Sigma,\mu)\) be a finite measure space. Then Proposition 3.9 shows that

\(\displaystyle\{L_{1}(X,\tilde{\Sigma},\mu):\tilde{\Sigma}\subseteq\Sigma\text{ countably generated }\sigma\text{-algebra}\}\)

is a rich family of closed separable subspaces of \(L_{1}(X,\Sigma,\mu)\).

Let \(X\) be a Banach space and let \(\mathcal{R}_{n}\) be a rich family of closed separable subspaces of \(X\) for each \(n\in\mathbb{N}\). Then

\(\mathcal{R}:=\bigcap_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\mathcal{R}_{n}\)

is a rich family of closed separable subspaces of \(X\).

Let \((X,\Sigma,\mu)\) and \((Y,\Gamma,\nu)\) be measure spaces of finite measure. Then the following assertions hold:

  1. (i)

    For any operator \(T:L_{1}(X,\Sigma,\mu)\to L_{1}(Y,\Gamma,\nu)\) the family

    \(\displaystyle\mathcal{R}_{T}:=\{E:\hskip 3.0pt\) \(\displaystyle E=L_{1}(X,\tilde{\Sigma},\mu)\text{ for }\tilde{\Sigma}\subseteq\Sigma\text{ countably generated }\sigma\text{-algebra},\)
    \(\displaystyle\text{and }|TJ_{E}|=|T|J_{E}\}\)

    is a rich family of closed separable subspaces of \(L_{1}(X,\Sigma,\mu)\).

  2. (ii)

    For a sequence of operators \((T_{s})_{s\in\mathbb{N}}\)

    \(\mathcal{R}:=\bigcap_{s\in\mathbb{N}}\mathcal{R}_{T_{s}}\)

    is a rich family of closed separable subspaces of \(L_{1}(X,\Sigma,\mu)\), where \(\mathcal{R}_{T_{s}}\) is defined as in (i).

Let \((X,\Sigma,\mu)\) and \((Y,\Gamma,\nu)\) be measure spaces of finite measure and let \(S:L_{1}(X,\Sigma,\mu)\to L_{1}(Y,\Gamma,\nu)\) be a singular operator. Then

\(\displaystyle\mathcal{R}^{S}=\{E\times F:\) \(\displaystyle\hskip 3.0ptE=L_{1}(X,\tilde{\Sigma},\mu)\text{ and }F=L_{1}(Y,\tilde{\Gamma},\nu)\text{ for some }\tilde{\Sigma}\subseteq\Sigma,\tilde{\Gamma}\subseteq\Gamma\)
\(\displaystyle\text{ countably generated }\sigma\text{-algebras, }S(E)\subseteq F,\)
\(\displaystyle\text{ and }S:E\rightarrow F\text{ is singular }\}\)

is a rich family of closed separable subspaces of \(L_{1}(X,\Sigma,\mu)\times L_{1}(Y,\Gamma,\nu)\).

Let \((X,\Sigma,\mu)\) and \((Y,\Gamma,\nu)\) be measure spaces of finite measure and \(S:L_{1}(X,\Sigma,\mu)\to L_{1}(Y,\Gamma,\nu)\) be a singular operator. Then we have

\(\Delta(S)=\lVert S\rVert=\lVert S\rVert_{w}.\)

Let \((X,\Sigma,\mu)\) and \((Y,\Gamma,\nu)\) be measure spaces of finite measure and \(K:L_{1}(X,\Sigma,\mu)\to L_{1}(Y,\Gamma,\nu)\) be an integral operator with kernel \(k\). Let \(\varepsilon>0\), then for each \(n\in\mathbb{N}\) we can find \(G_{n}\subseteq Y\) with \(\nu(G_{n})\leq\frac{2\rVert K\lVert}{n}\) and \(M_{n}\in\Sigma\) of positive measure such that

\(\int_{G_{n}}|k(x,y)|d\nu(y)\geq\int_{Y}|k_{n}(x,y)|d\nu(y)-\varepsilon\text{ for all }x\in M_{n},\)

where \(k_{n}\) are the truncated kernels of \(k\).

The previous decomposition as an \(\ell_{1}\)-sum is actually valid for any measure space \((X,\Sigma,\mu)\), if one allows the sets \((X_{i})_{i\in I}\) to form an almost decomposition, in the sense that

\(\mu(X_{i}\cap X_{j})=0\quad\text{for all }i\neq j.\)

Details of such a construction can be found, for example, in . Therefore, even the concrete formulas we prove for measures remain valid for arbitrary measure spaces \((X,\Sigma,\mu)\), with only minor modifications of the proofs. For simplicity of presentation, we state and prove the results in the case of strictly localizable measure spaces. We thank the referee for pointing out that the results can naturally be extended to arbitrary measure spaces.

Let \((X,\Sigma,\mu)\) be a measure space of finite measure and \((Y,\Gamma,\nu)\) be a strictly localizable measure space with decomposition \(((Y_{j},\Sigma_{j},\nu))_{j\in J}\). Then the range of any operator \(T:L_{1}(X,\Sigma,\mu)\to L_{1}(Y,\Gamma,\nu)\) is contained in the direct sum of \(L_{1}(Y_{j},\Gamma_{j},\nu)\) for at most countably many \(j\in J\).

The reader is advised to exercise caution when analyzing this situation, as many standard results do not automatically carry over if one attempts to directly extend Definition 3.11 to strictly localizable measure spaces. For instance, in the previous calculation, we used Tonelli’s theorem to conclude that the kernels of \(K^{(i)}\) and \((K^{(i)})^{*}\) coincide. This relies on the spaces being \(\sigma\)-finite, and may fail in a more general setting.

The condition that \(\nu(\Theta)<\infty\) is crucial to guarantee that \(\alpha_{\Theta}\) is a good measure of weak compactness. Further, observe that if \(Y\) has finite measure, then taking \(\Theta=Y\) gives \(\alpha_{\Theta}(T)=\Delta(T)\), that is, we recover the modulus of equi-integrability.

Let \((X,\Sigma,\mu)\) and \((Y,\Gamma,\nu)\) be strictly localizable measure spaces and \(T:L_{1}(X,\Sigma,\mu)\to L_{1}(Y,\Gamma,\nu)\) be an operator. Then for any measurable subset \(\Theta\subseteq Y\) of finite measure, we have

\(\alpha_{\Theta}(T)\leq\lVert T\rVert_{w,\Theta}.\)

Let \((X,\Sigma,\mu)\) and \((Y,\Gamma,\nu)\) be strictly localizable measure spaces and \(T:L_{1}(X,\Sigma,\mu)\to L_{1}(Y,\Gamma,\nu)\) be an operator. Express \(T=S+K\) where \(S\) is a singular operator and \(K\) is an integral operator with kernel \(k\). Then for any measurable subset \(\Theta\subseteq Y\) of finite measure, we have

\(\alpha_{\Theta}(T)=\inf_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\operatorname*{ess\,sup}_{x\in X}\{|S^{*}|\mathds{1}_{Y}(x)+\int_{Y\backslash\Theta}|k(x,y)|d\nu(y)+\int_{\Theta}|k_{n}(x,y)|d\nu(y)\},\)

where \(k_{n}\) are the truncated kernels of the operator \(K\).

Let \((X,\Sigma,\mu)\) and \((Y,\Gamma,\nu)\) be strictly localizable measure spaces and \(T:L_{1}(X,\Sigma,\mu)\to L_{1}(Y,\Gamma,\nu)\) be an operator. Then for any measurable subset \(\Theta\subseteq Y\) of finite measure, there exists a weakly compact operator \(H\) with range in \(L_{1}(\Theta,\gamma,\nu)\) such that

\(\lVert T-H\rVert=\lVert T\rVert_{w,\Theta}=\alpha_{\Theta}(T).\)

Let \((X,\Sigma,\mu)\) and \((Y,\Gamma,\nu)\) be strictly localizable measure spaces and \(T:L_{1}(X,\Sigma,\mu)\to L_{1}(Y,\Gamma,\nu)\) be an operator. Then for any measurable subsets \(\Pi\subseteq\Theta\subseteq Y\) of finite measure, we have

\(\alpha_{\Theta}(T)\leq\alpha_{\Pi}(T).\)

results.title: (General finite measure case).
results.statementHtml:
Let \((X,\Sigma,\mu)\) and \((Y,\Gamma,\nu)\) be measure spaces of finite measure. Then there exists a weakly compact operator \(H\) such that

\(\lVert T-H\rVert=\lVert T\rVert=\Delta(T).\)

Let \((X,\Sigma,\mu)\) and \((Y,\Gamma,\nu)\) be strictly localizable measure spaces and \(W:L_{1}(X,\Sigma,\mu)\to L_{1}(Y,\Gamma,\nu)\) be a weakly compact operator. Then there exists a \(\sigma\)-finite measurable set \(\Theta\subseteq Y\), such that

\(W[L_{1}(X,\Sigma,\mu)]\subseteq L_{1}(\Theta,\gamma,\nu),\)

where recall \(\gamma=\{A\cap\Theta:A\in\Sigma\}\).

Let \((X,\Sigma,\mu)\) and \((Y,\Gamma,\nu)\) be strictly localizable measure spaces and \(T:L_{1}(X,\Sigma,\mu)\to L_{1}(Y,\Gamma,\nu)\) be an operator. Then for any \(\sigma\)-finite measurable set \(\Theta\subseteq Y\), there exists a weakly compact operator \(H\) with range in \(L_{1}(\Theta,\gamma,\nu)\), where \(\gamma=\{A\cap\Theta:A\in\Gamma\}\), such that

\(\lVert T-H\rVert=\lVert T\rVert_{w,\Theta}.\)

Let \((X,\Sigma,\mu)\) and \((Y,\Gamma,\nu)\) be strictly localizable measure spaces, and \(T:L_{1}(X,\Sigma,\mu)\to L_{1}(Y,\Gamma,\nu)\) be an operator. Then there exists a weakly compact operator \(H:L_{1}(X,\Sigma,\mu)\to L_{1}(Y,\Gamma,\nu)\) such that

\(\lVert T\rVert_{w}=\lVert T-H\rVert.\)

Let \((Y,\Gamma,\nu)\) be a strictly localizable measurable space, \(g\in L_{1}(Y,\Gamma,\nu)\) and \(\Pi,\Theta\subseteq Y\) measurable sets of finite measure.

Then, for every \(\varepsilon>0\), there exists a measurable subset of finite measure \(\Theta_{\varepsilon}\subseteq Y\) such that \(\Pi\cup\Theta\subseteq\Theta_{\varepsilon}\) and

\(\lVert\chi_{\Theta_{\varepsilon}\backslash\Theta}g-\chi_{Y\backslash\Theta}g\rVert<\varepsilon.\)

Let \((X,\Sigma,\mu)\) and \((Y,\Gamma,\nu)\) be strictly localizable measure spaces, and \(T:L_{1}(X,\Sigma,\mu)\to L_{1}(Y,\Gamma,\nu)\) be an operator. Denote

\(\beta=\inf_{\Theta\subseteq Y,\nu(\Theta)<\infty}\alpha_{\Theta}(T).\)

Then there exist an increasing sequence of sets of finite measure \(\Theta_{n}\subseteq Y\), a sequence \(B_{n}\subseteq\Theta_{n}\) of measurable sets with \(\nu(B_{n})\to 0\) and a sequence of norm one elements \((f_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\subseteq L_{1}(X,\Sigma,\mu)\) such that

\(\lim_{n\to\infty}\lVert\chi_{\Theta_{n+1}\backslash\Theta_{n}}T-\chi_{B_{n}}T\rVert=\lim_{n\to\infty}\lVert\chi_{\Theta_{n+1}\backslash\Theta_{n}}Tf_{n}-\chi_{B_{n}}Tf_{n}\rVert=\lim_{n\to\infty}\alpha_{\Theta_{n}}(T)=\beta.\)

Let \((X,\Sigma,\mu)\) and \((Y,\Gamma,\nu)\) be strictly localizable measure spaces, and \(T:L_{1}(X,\Sigma,\mu)\to L_{1}(Y,\Gamma,\nu)\) be an operator. Then

\(\lVert T\rVert_{w}=\inf_{\Theta\subseteq Y,\nu(\Theta)<\infty}\alpha_{\Theta}(T).\)

Let \((X,\Sigma,\mu)\) and \((Y,\Gamma,\nu)\) be strictly localizable measurable spaces, and \(T:L_{1}(X,\Sigma,\mu)\to L_{1}(Y,\Gamma,\nu)\) be a non-weakly compact operator. Then there exist a sequence \((f_{n})_{n=1}^{\infty}\subseteq L_{1}(X,\Sigma,\mu)\) of norm one functions and pairwise disjoint sets \((A_{n})_{n=1}^{\infty}\subseteq\Gamma\) of finite measure such that

\(\lim_{n\to\infty}\lVert\chi_{A_{n}}Tf_{n}\rVert\geq\lVert T\rVert_{w}\)

Let \(E\) be a Banach space and \((x_{n})_{n=1}^{\infty}\subseteq E\) be a weakly convergent sequence. Then there exist an increasing sequence of natural numbers \((i_{n})_{n=1}^{\infty}\) and a sequence of scalars \((\alpha_{i})_{i=1}^{\infty}\) satisfying

  1. (i)

    \(\sum_{i=i_{n}+1}^{i_{n+1}}|\alpha_{i}|=1\),

  2. (ii)

    the sequence \((x_{n}^{\prime})_{n=1}^{\infty}\) defined by \(x_{n}^{\prime}=\sum_{i=i_{n}+1}^{i_{n+1}}\alpha_{i}x_{i}\) converges in norm to \(0\).

results.title: (Subsequence Splitting Lemma).
results.statementHtml:
Let \((X,\Sigma,\mu)\) be a measure space of finite measure and \((f_{n})_{n=1}^{\infty}\) be a bounded sequence in \(L_{1}(X,\Sigma,\mu)\). Then, there exist a subsequence \((f_{n_{k}})_{k=1}^{\infty}\) and two other sequences \((g_{k})_{k=1}^{\infty}\), \((h_{k})_{k=1}^{\infty}\) such that the following three assertions hold:

  • (i)

    \(f_{n_{k}}=g_{k}+h_{k}\) for all \(k\in\mathbb{N}\),

  • (ii)

    \(\inf\left(|g_{k}|,|h_{k}|\right)=0=\inf\left(|h_{\ell}|,|h_{m}|\right)\quad\text{for all }k,\ \text{and all }\ell\neq m\),

  • (iii)

    \((g_{k})_{k=1}^{\infty}\) is weakly convergent.

A sequence \((f_{n})_{n=1}^{\infty}\) in \(L_{1}(X,\Sigma,\mu)\) is called disjoint if \(|f_{n}|\wedge|f_{m}|=0\) whenever \(m\not=n\). A sequence \((g_{n})_{n=1}^{\infty}\) in \(L_{1}(X,\Sigma,\mu)\) is called almost disjoint if there exists a disjoint sequence \((f_{n})_{n=1}^{\infty}\) satisfying \(\lVert f_{n}-g_{n}\rVert\to 0\) as \(n\to\infty\).

Let \((X,\Sigma,\mu)\) and \((Y,\Gamma,\nu)\) be strictly localizable measure spaces and \(T:L_{1}(X,\Sigma,\mu)\to L_{1}(Y,\Gamma,\nu)\) be a non-weakly compact operator. Then there exists a disjoint sequence \((u_{n})_{n=1}^{\infty}\subseteq L_{1}(X,\Sigma,\mu)\) with \(\lVert u_{n}\rVert=1\) such that \((Tu_{n})_{n=1}^{\infty}\) is almost disjoint and \(\lVert Tu_{n}\rVert\to\lVert T\rVert_{w}\).

By , \(L_{1}[0,1]\) does not have the weak approximation property, and thus by , there exists a Banach space \(F\) such that \(\lVert\cdot\rVert_{w}\) and \(\omega(\cdot)\) are not equivalent, where recall that \(\omega(\cdot)\) is the De Blasi measure of weak noncompactness (1). In particular, we can find a sequence of operators \(T_{n}:F\to L_{1}[0,1]\) with \(\lVert T_{n}\rVert_{w}=1\) and

\(\sup\{\lVert U\rVert^{-1}\lVert V\rVert^{-1}:UT_{n}V=I_{\ell_{1}}\}\leq\omega(T_{n})<1/n,\)

where the first inequality follows since for any \(U,V\) such that \(UT_{n}V=I_{\ell_{1}}\) we have

\(1=\omega(I_{\ell_{1}})=\omega(UT_{n}V)\leq\lVert U\rVert\lVert V\rVert\omega(T_{n}),\)

that is \(\omega(T_{n})\geq\lVert U\rVert^{-1}\lVert V\rVert^{-1}\). This shows that no such quantitative factorizations are possible using the weak essential norm.

Incidentally, the same reasoning yields an identical conclusion for any \(AL\)-space without the Schur property, showing that no general factorization is possible in that case either. On the other hand, if an \(AL\)-space \(E\) has the Schur property, then \(E\cong\ell_{1}(\Gamma)\) for some set \(\Gamma\). In this case, such a factorization is easily achieved, independently of the domain of the operator.

A function \(\alpha:\mathscr{B}(E)\to[0,\infty)\) is said to be a measure of weak noncompactness if it satisfies:

  1. (a)

    \(\alpha(T+S)\leq\alpha(T)+\alpha(S)\) and \(\alpha(\lambda T)=|\lambda|\alpha(T)\) for all \(T,S\in\mathscr{B}(E)\) and \(\lambda\in\mathbb{K}\).

  2. (b)

    \(\alpha(TS)\leq\min\{\lVert T\rVert\alpha(S),\alpha(T)\lVert S\rVert\}\) for all \(T,S\in\mathscr{B}(E)\).

  3. (c)

    \(\alpha(T)=0\) if and only if \(T\) is weakly compact.

  4. (d)

    There exist \(J_{\ell_{1}}:\ell_{1}\to E\) an isometric inclusion and \(\pi_{\ell_{1}}:E\to\ell_{1}\) a norm one operator, satisfying \(\pi_{\ell_{1}}J_{\ell_{1}}=I_{\ell_{1}}\) and \(\alpha(J_{\ell_{1}}\pi_{\ell_{1}})\geq 1\).

We will say that \(\alpha\) is normalized if, additionally, we have \(\alpha(I_{E})=1\).

In (d), we emphasise that it suffices to exhibit any such \(J_{\ell_{1}}\) and \(\pi_{\ell_{1}}\). In terms of set measures of weak noncompactness, this condition says that the unit ball of \(\ell_{1}\) has measure at least \(1\).

Let \(\alpha\) be a normalized measure of weak noncompactness and \(T\in\mathscr{B}(E)\). Then

\(\alpha(T)\leq\lVert T\rVert_{w}.\)
Let \(\alpha\) be a normalized measure of weak noncompactness and \(T\in\mathscr{B}(E)\). Then \(\alpha(T)=\lVert T\rVert_{w}\).

Corollary 1.11 could also have been obtained by mimicking the arguments in the proof of . However, since the general form of the result for normalized measures of weak noncompactness will be needed later, and because other notions (not necessarily algebra norms) have been extensively studied in the literature, we have chosen to prove it starting from the more general formulation.

The De Blasi measure of weak noncompactness \(\omega(\cdot)\), when applied to operators, is a normalised measure of weak noncompactness in the sense of Definition 5.8. The only non-trivial property to verify is (b). Let \(S,T:E\to E\) be bounded linear operators. Since \(SB_{E}\subseteq\|S\|B_{E}\), we have

\(\omega(TS)=\omega\bigl(T(SB_{E})\bigr)\leq\omega\bigl(T(\|S\|B_{E})\bigr)=\|S\|\,\omega\bigl(TB_{E}\bigr)=\|S\|\,\omega(T).\)

Thus, it suffices to prove the general inequality

\(\omega(TA)\leq\|T\|\,\omega(A)\qquad\text{for every bounded set }A\subseteq E.\)

Fix \(\varepsilon>\omega(A)\). By definition of \(\omega(A)\) there exists a weakly compact set \(D\subseteq E\) such that

\(A\subseteq D+\varepsilon B_{E}.\)

Since bounded linear operators are weak-to-weak continuous, \(T(D)\) is weakly compact. Applying \(T\) to the inclusion above yields

\(TA\subseteq T(D)+\varepsilon\,T(B_{E})\subseteq T(D)+\varepsilon\,\|T\|B_{E}.\)

Thus

\(\omega(TA)\leq\varepsilon\|T\|.\)

As this holds for all \(\varepsilon>\omega(A)\), we obtain

\(\omega(TA)\leq\|T\|\,\omega(A).\)

Applying this with \(A=SB_{E}\), we conclude that

\(\omega(TS)=\omega(TSB_{E})\leq\|T\|\,\omega(SB_{E})=\|T\|\,\omega(S),\)

which verifies property (b) for the De Blasi measure of weak noncompactness.

Let \(E=L_{1}(X,\Sigma,\mu)\) for a strictly localizable measure space and \(T\in\mathscr{B}(E)\). Then we have

\(\displaystyle\lVert T\rVert_{w}\) \(\displaystyle=\inf_{\Theta\subseteq Y,\nu(\Theta)<\infty}\alpha_{\Theta}(T)=\omega(TB_{E})=\operatorname{wk}_{E}(TB_{E})=\operatorname{wck}_{E}(TB_{E})\)
\(\displaystyle=\inf_{c>0,\mu(E)<\infty}\sup\{\int_{X}(|Tf|-c\mathds{1}_{E})^{+}d\mu(x):f\in B_{E}\}.\)

In the case that \(\mu\) is finite, this simplifies to

\(\displaystyle\lVert T\rVert_{w}\) \(\displaystyle=\Delta(T)=\omega(TB_{E})=\operatorname{wk}_{E}(TB_{E})=\operatorname{wck}_{E}(TB_{E})\)
\(\displaystyle=\inf_{c>0}\sup\{\int_{X}(|Tf|-c)^{+}d\mu(x):f\in B_{E})\}.\)

Let \(K\) be a compact Hausdorff space, and let \(A\subseteq\mathcal{M}(K)\) be a bounded subset. The modulus of uniform regularity of \(A\) is defined by

\(\varepsilon(A)=\sup\left\{\inf_{n\in\mathbb{N}}|\mu_{n}|(U_{n}):(U_{n})_{n=1}^{\infty}\text{ disjoint open subsets of }K,\ (\mu_{n})_{n=1}^{\infty}\subseteq A\right\}.\)

Let \(K\) be a compact Hausdorff space. Then for any operator \(T:\mathcal{M}(K)\to\mathcal{M}(K)\) we have

\(\varepsilon(TB_{\mathcal{M}(K)})=\omega(TB_{\mathcal{M}(K)})=\lVert T\rVert_{w}.\)

Let \(T:C(K)\to C(L)\) be an operator, where \(K,L\) are compact Hausdorff spaces. Then

\(\lVert T^{*}\rVert_{w}=\sup\{m(TV)|\hskip 5.0ptV:c_{0}\to C(L),\hskip 5.0pt\lVert V\rVert\leq 1\}.\)

The quantity

\(\sup\{m(TV)\;|\;V:c_{0}\to C(L),\;\|V\|\leq 1\},\)

which measures how well an operator \(T\) fixes a copy of \(c_{0}\), has also been studied for operators between arbitrary Banach spaces \(T:X\to Y\). For example, in this quantity appears under the name \(\operatorname{fix}_{c_{0}}(T)\), and it is shown that

\(\operatorname{fix}_{c_{0}}(T)=\operatorname{uc}(T)\)

, where \(\operatorname{uc}(T)\) quantifies how far \(T\) is from being unconditionally converging. Moreover, it is shown that for operators \(T:C(K)\to Y\), this quantity coincides with several other measures of weak noncompactness, see . In particular, Proposition 6.3 may be viewed as an extension of the aforementioned corollary in the case where the codomain is also a \(C(K)\)-space.

results.title: (Dowling, Randrianantoanina and Turett).
results.statementHtml: Let \(E\) be a Banach space. Suppose there exists \(M\subseteq B_{E^{*}}\) \(1\)-norming and weak∗ sequentially compact. Then for any \(Y\subseteq E\), \(Y\sim c_{0}\) and any \(\varepsilon>0\), there exist \(Z\subseteq Y\) and a projection \(P:E\to Z\) such that \(Z\) is \((1+\varepsilon)\)-isometric to \(c_{0}\) and \(\lVert P\rVert\leq 1+\varepsilon\).

The previous reformulation is stronger than the original version by Dowling, Randrianantoanina, and Turett, particularly in the context of \(C(K)\)-spaces. Indeed, the set \(\{\delta_{k}:k\in K\}\subseteq C(K)^{*}\) is always \(1\)-norming, so the existence of a \(1\)-norming, weak∗ sequentially compact subset of the dual unit ball is automatically satisfied whenever \(K\) is sequentially compact. In contrast, requiring the dual unit ball to be weak∗ sequentially compact can be a stronger condition. For instance, assuming the Continuum Hypothesis, Talagrand constructed a Corson compact space \(K\) that is first countable, and hence sequentially compact, but for which the unit ball of \(C(K)^{*}\) (endowed with the weak∗ topology) contains a topological copy of \(\beta\mathbb{N}\) (see ). In particular, the dual unit ball fails to be sequentially compact while \(K\) is sequentially compact. We thank Antonio Avilés for bringing this example to our attention.

results.title: (Rosenthal).
results.statementHtml: Let \(\Gamma\) be an infinite set, and let \(E\) and \(F\) be Banach spaces with \(E\) \(1\)-complemented in \(E^{**}\). Let \(T:E\to F\) and \(V:c_{0}\to E\), \(\lVert V\rVert\leq 1\), such that \(m(TV)>\delta\). Then there exists \(\tilde{V}:\ell_{\infty}\to E\) such that \(T\tilde{V}:\ell_{\infty}\to F\) satisfies \(m(T\tilde{V})>\delta\).
